title: How water climbs a plant, from the roots to the leaves

summary.text: A tree has no heart and no pump, yet water reaches the leaves at the very top. Water enters a plant through the roots and climbs the stem in tiny tubes called xylem. Most of it then evaporates out of tiny holes in the leaves. As water leaves the top, it pulls up the water below it, because water molecules attract each other. The Sun's heat makes the water evaporate, so the energy for the lift comes from the Sun. Your child stands a pale cabbage leaf or a white flower in coloured water, and within a day finds the colour in its veins. They also meet Jagadish Chandra Bose, who thought living cells pumped the water up, and the evidence that it is pulled instead.
summary.art: A cut-away drawing of a tulsi plant in a pot: tiny blue drops entering root hairs, climbing a glowing tube inside the stem, spreading through the leaf veins and floating out of the leaves as faint mist towards a warm Sun.

intro.hook: Look at a tall coconut palm or a neem tree. Their top leaves need water, but the water is in the soil, far below. Nobody carries it up, and a tree has no heart and no pump. So how does the water get to the top?
intro.text: Try this today. Stir lots of food colour into half a glass of water. Stand a pale inner leaf of a cabbage in it, thick white rib down, or a white carnation. Look again after a few hours, and the next day. If thin coloured lines appear in the leaf or the petals, the coloured water has climbed up inside. Water makes this journey in every plant, from the roots to the very top leaf.
intro.art: A pale cabbage leaf and a white carnation standing in a glass of deep blue water on a windowsill, and the next day the same leaf with blue veins and the flower with blue-edged petals.

outcomes: I can trace the path of water through a plant: into the roots, up the stem, and out to the leaves and flowers.
I can set up the coloured-water experiment, keep it a fair test, and use what I see as evidence that a stem has tubes inside.
I can explain that leaves let water out into the air as invisible vapour, and that this pulls more water up the stem.
I can explain why a plant wilts, how to help them, and why flower sellers cut stems again under water.
I can measure how fast water climbs or is used up, and show my results in a table and a bar chart.
I can say what scientists agree on about how water climbs a tall tree, what they argued about, and what is still unknown.
I can explain why a thread of water does not snap as it climbs, and where the energy to lift it comes from.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that grows into the soil. It holds the plant firm and soaks up water.
terms.example: Pull up a weed gently. The white threads at the bottom are the weed's roots.
terms.art: A small weed lifted from the soil with their white roots hanging down.

terms.meaning: A very thin, fuzzy hair on a young root. Each one is a single long cell. Root hairs push between grains of soil and soak up water.
terms.example: Sprout a moong seed on a wet cloth. The white fuzz on their root is root hairs.
terms.art: A moong sprout seen through a magnifying glass, their root covered in white fuzz.

terms.meaning: To soak something up, the way a sponge soaks up water.
terms.example: Roots absorb water from wet soil.
terms.art: A sponge corner dipped in water, the water creeping up into it.

terms.meaning: The part that holds a plant up. It carries water up from the roots to the leaves and flowers. A tree's trunk is a big, woody stem.
terms.example: The long stalk of a rajnigandha flower, or of a balsam plant, is the stem.
terms.art: A balsam plant with their see-through green stem highlighted.

terms.meaning: To carry something from one place to another.
terms.example: A truck transports vegetables to the market. A stem transports water to the leaves.
terms.art: A vegetable truck on a road beside a plant stem with water drops moving up it.

terms.meaning: The tiny water tubes inside a plant. They run from the roots, up the stem, and into every leaf. Most are thinner than a hair.
terms.example: The tough strings in a stick of sugarcane or a banana stem are bundles that hold xylem tubes.
terms.art: The thick white rib of a cabbage leaf cut across, showing a row of coloured dots, each dot a bundle of tubes.

terms.meaning: A line you can see on a leaf or petal. Veins hold the water tubes that bring water to every part of the leaf.
terms.example: Hold a peepal leaf up to the light. The lines are its veins.
terms.art: A peepal leaf held up against the sun, its veins glowing like a map of roads.

terms.meaning: When a liquid turns into a gas. Water that evaporates becomes invisible water vapour and mixes into the air.
terms.example: Wet clothes on a line dry because the water evaporates.
terms.art: Clothes drying on a line in the sun with faint wavy lines rising from them.

terms.meaning: Water as an invisible gas in the air. When it cools, it turns back into drops.
terms.example: A cold steel tumbler gets drops on the outside. They come from water vapour in the air.
terms.art: A cold steel tumbler with water droplets on its outside.

terms.meaning: Water leaving a plant's leaves as invisible vapour. As water leaves the top of the plant, it pulls more water up the stem.
terms.example: Tie a clear bag over a leafy branch. After an hour, the inside is misty. That is transpiration.
terms.art: A clear plastic bag tied over a leafy branch, misty and dotted with drops inside.

terms.meaning: A tiny hole in a leaf, far too small to see without a microscope. One hole is a stoma. Many are stomata. Water vapour goes out of them, and air comes in.
terms.example: Most of a mango leaf's stomata are on its underside.
terms.art: A microscope view of a leaf's underside, with many small mouth-shaped holes.

terms.meaning: Two curved cells around each leaf hole, like two lips. They open the hole or close it.
terms.example: On a very hot, dry afternoon, guard cells often close the holes so the plant loses less water.
terms.art: A close-up of one leaf hole with two bean-shaped guard cells, shown open and then closed.

terms.meaning: When a plant goes floppy and droops because they are losing water faster than they can drink.
terms.example: Coriander left out of the fridge on a hot day wilts.
terms.art: A bunch of coriander drooping over the edge of a kitchen counter.

terms.meaning: Firm and stiff because the cells are full of water. Full cells push against each other like water balloons packed in a bag, so stems and leaves stand up.
terms.example: Fresh palak leaves are crisp and turgid. Old ones go limp.
terms.art: A bag packed tight with small water balloons beside a crisp spinach leaf.

terms.meaning: The smallest piece of something that is still that thing. A water molecule is made of three atoms: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
terms.example: Scientists estimate that one drop of water has more molecules than there are grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth.
terms.art: A water drop with a zoom circle showing tiny water molecules, each a big ball with two smaller balls stuck on.

terms.meaning: Water molecules attracting each other, so that water holds together. It is why water forms round drops.
terms.example: A drop of water on a leaf stays round, because its molecules hold on to each other.
terms.art: A long chain of cartoon water molecules holding hands, climbing up a thin tube.

terms.meaning: Water creeping up into very thin gaps by itself, because it sticks to the sides of the gap.
terms.example: Dip the corner of a tissue in tea. The tea climbs up the tissue.
terms.art: A tissue corner dipped in a cup of tea, the brown colour creeping upwards.

terms.meaning: A small push from the roots that squeezes water a little way up the stem, mostly at night.
terms.example: On some mornings, grass tips have tiny beads of water squeezed out of them.
terms.art: Blades of grass at dawn, each tip holding one bright bead of water.

terms.meaning: The plant's second set of tubes. They carry sugary food made in the leaves to the rest of the plant. This unit is about the water tubes, the xylem.
terms.example: Sugarcane juice is sweet because the cane stores food carried in its phloem.
terms.art: A stem cut open showing two kinds of tubes side by side, one with blue drops and one with golden sugar.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing, and keep everything else the same. Then you know what caused the difference.
terms.example: Two mint stems in the same bottles of water, one with leaves and one without. Only the leaves are different.
terms.art: Two identical narrow bottles of water, one with a leafy mint stem and one with a bare mint stem.

terms.meaning: What you saw or measured that shows your idea is true, or not true.
terms.example: Blue lines in a white petal are evidence that coloured water climbed up the stem.
terms.art: A child pointing at blue lines in a white flower's petals, a notebook open beside it.

explanations.concept: The path of water: root, stem, leaf, air
explanations.definition: Water enters a plant through the roots. It travels up the stem in tiny tubes. It spreads through the veins to every leaf and flower. Most of it then leaves through tiny holes in the leaves, as invisible vapour.
explanations.description: The path starts in the soil, where root hairs soak up water. The water moves into the root and then up the stem, inside bundles of very fine tubes. In each leaf, the tubes branch out along the veins. From the veins, water soaks into the leaf's cells. It evaporates into tiny air spaces inside the leaf, and the vapour escapes through tiny holes in the leaf's skin. Some water stays behind, to keep the plant firm and to help the leaves make food. The photosynthesis unit tells that part of the story.
examples: Water a tulsi pot. The water goes into the roots, not the leaves.
A banana leaf's veins run from its thick middle rib out to the edges, carrying water across the leaf.
On a hot day a neem tree sends water from deep soil to leaves higher than a house.
explanations.art: A labelled path drawn on a plant: 1 root hairs in soil, 2 tubes in the stem, 3 veins in the leaf, 4 mist leaving the leaf into the air.
explanations.context: This card gives the big picture of the whole unit: the path one drop of water takes through a plant.

explanations.concept: The tubes inside a stem: xylem
explanations.definition: Xylem is the set of tiny tubes that carry water from the roots to the leaves. They run the whole length of the plant, and into every vein.
explanations.description: A stem is not a solid stick. Inside, it is packed with bundles of tubes. Most of them are thinner than a hair. Each tube is made of cells that have died and lost their insides. Their end walls opened up, so the cells join into long hollow pipes, like cups with no bottoms stacked one on top of another. When you stand a white flower or a cabbage leaf in coloured water and then cut it across, each coloured dot is one bundle of tubes. In a tree, the xylem is the wood itself. In places with a cold or a dry season, the tree adds a new ring of water tubes every year.
examples: The tough strings in a stick of sugarcane or a banana stem are bundles of tubes.
The rings in a cut tree trunk are layers of old water tubes, one for each year.
The lines on a white carnation's petals fill with colour when its stem stands in coloured water for a day.
explanations.art: A zoom in three steps: a white flower stem, its cut end with a ring of blue dots, then one dot opened up into a bundle of hollow tubes like stacked bottomless cups.
explanations.context: You cannot see water climbing inside a plant. This card explains the hidden tubes it climbs through.

explanations.definition: Transpiration is water leaving a plant through tiny holes in their leaves, called stomata, as invisible water vapour.
explanations.description: Each leaf is covered in tiny holes, far too small to see. A patch of leaf the size of your little fingernail can have thousands of them. Each hole has two curved guard cells around it, which open and close it. When the holes open, air comes in. The leaf needs a gas from the air, called carbon dioxide, to make its food. But while the holes are open, water vapour escapes too. The plant cannot let carbon dioxide in without letting water out. That is why most of the water a plant takes up goes back into the air.
examples: A clear bag tied over a leafy branch turns misty inside within an hour in the sun.
A potted plant covered with a clear jar in the sun gets drops on the inside of the jar.
A cactus has very few holes, and opens them mostly at night, when the air is cool.
explanations.art: A leaf seen up close with tiny mouth-shaped holes on its underside, faint wisps of vapour leaving some of them.
explanations.context: Where does the water go when it reaches the leaves? This card explains that most of it leaves through tiny holes, into the air.

explanations.definition: Water is pulled up a plant from the top. As water evaporates from the leaves, it tugs on the water behind it. Because water molecules hold on to each other, the whole thread of water in each tube moves up.
explanations.description: Imagine a long line of children holding hands, standing up a staircase. The child at the top lets go and runs off. Everyone else steps up one stair to close the gap. A new child joins at the bottom. That is how water climbs a plant. Each water tube holds one unbroken thread of water, from the roots to a leaf. When a bit of water evaporates from the leaf, the thread is pulled up a little. New water is soaked up at the roots to fill the bottom. Scientists call this the cohesion-tension idea. Cohesion means water sticking to itself. Tension means a pull, like a stretched rope.
examples: A leafy stem pulls water up faster than a stem with its leaves taken off.
Trees drink most in the hot, sunny middle of the day, when their leaves lose the most water.
Drinking through a straw looks similar, but there the air outside pushes the drink up. In a tree, the water really is pulled from the top.
explanations.art: A line of children holding hands up a staircase inside a tree trunk. At the top, one child skips off into the air as a little cloud, and the rest step up.
explanations.context: This card explains how water climbs up a plant, all the way to the top leaf, with no pump.

explanations.concept: An old argument: push, pump or pull?
explanations.description: For more than 150 years, scientists argued about how water reaches the top of a tree. Some thought the roots pushed it. Some thought living cells pumped it. Some thought the leaves pulled it. Today, almost all plant scientists agree that the pull from the leaves does most of the work. Sometimes the roots give a small push too. The argument was settled by experiments, not by who was most famous.
examples: Cut a grapevine stem in spring and sap drips out of the stump. That drip is a push from the roots.
Coloured water still climbs up a stem whose living cells have been killed. So living pumps are not needed.

perspectives.who: Stephen Hales, an English clergyman and scientist, in his book Vegetable Staticks, 1727
perspectives.explanation: He weighed potted plants and measured how much water they lost through their leaves each day. He also fixed glass tubes to cut vine stems and saw sap pushed up the tubes. He showed that roots can push, and that leaves lose a lot of water.

perspectives.who: Eduard Strasburger, a German botanist, in 1891
perspectives.explanation: He killed the living cells in long stems with poison and heat. Coloured liquid still climbed up them. So whatever lifts the water does not need living cells along the way.

perspectives.who: Henry Dixon and John Joly, two scientists in Dublin, Ireland, in 1894
perspectives.explanation: Water is pulled up from the top. Leaves let water evaporate, and that tugs on unbroken threads of water in the tubes. Water molecules cling together so strongly that the threads do not snap. This is the idea accepted today.

perspectives.who: Jagadish Chandra Bose, an Indian scientist in Kolkata, in his book The Physiology of the Ascent of Sap, 1923
perspectives.explanation: A layer of living cells in the stem squeezes in a rhythm, like tiny hearts, and pumps the water upwards. He built clever instruments to show plants pulsing. Most scientists were not convinced, and this idea is now rejected. Bose is still honoured for showing that plants sense and respond.

explanations.art: Four small portraits in a row: Hales with a potted plant on a scale, Strasburger with a glass tube, Dixon and Joly with a tall tree diagram, Bose with his recording instrument.
explanations.context: Scientists argued for a long time about what lifts water up a tree. This card tells the story of that argument and who said what.

explanations.concept: Why plants wilt, and spring back
explanations.definition: A plant wilts when they lose water from their leaves faster than their roots can take water in. Their cells go soft, like half-empty water balloons, and the plant droops.
explanations.description: Most living plant cells have a stretchy bag inside, called a vacuole, that fills with water. When all the cells are full, they press hard against each other and against their walls. That pressing makes leaves and soft stems stand up firm. When water runs short, the cells go soft and floppy. Then the stem bends and the leaves hang down. Give a wilted plant water soon, and the cells fill up again. In an hour they can stand tall. But if they stay dry too long, the cells are damaged and they may not recover.
examples: Wilted coriander stood in a glass of water perks up within an hour or two.
Garden plants often droop in the hot afternoon, then stand up again in the cool evening.
A plant pulled up roughly wilts, because their root hairs are torn off and they cannot drink.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: a drooping balsam plant with cells drawn as soft half-empty balloons, and the same plant upright with plump full balloons.
explanations.context: Have you seen a plant droop on a hot day? This card explains what wilting is, and why water brings a plant back.

explanations.concept: What makes a plant drink faster
explanations.definition: A plant loses water faster, and so drinks faster, when it is sunny, warm, windy and dry. A plant loses water more slowly when it is dark, cool, still or damp.
explanations.description: Think about drying clothes. They dry fastest on a hot, sunny, windy day, and slowest on a damp, still night. Leaves lose water in the same way. Sunlight also makes most plants open their leaf holes, to let air in for making food. More leaves mean more holes, so a leafy stem drinks faster than a bare one. The chart shows made-up results from the leafy and bare stem test in this unit.
examples: A plant on a sunny balcony needs watering more often than one in a shady room.
Desert plants like cactus have few leaves, or none, so they lose less water.
Farmers in hot places often water in the early morning or evening, when less is lost to the air.
explanations.art: Four small pictures of the same potted plant: in hot sun with a fan blowing, in shade, at night under the Moon, and on a misty damp morning, with big or small vapour arrows.
explanations.context: Some days plants drink a lot and some days hardly at all. This card explains why, using a test you can do with two stems in water.

chart.title: Made-up example: how much the water level dropped in 2 days
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

explanations.definition: Water molecules attract each other. This is called cohesion. They also cling to the walls of thin tubes. This is called adhesion. Both come from tiny electric forces between molecules.
explanations.description: A water molecule is one oxygen atom with two hydrogen atoms stuck on. It looks a bit like a head with two ears. The oxygen end has a tiny bit of negative electric charge. The hydrogen ends have a tiny bit of positive charge. Opposite charges attract. So the hydrogen end of one molecule attracts the oxygen end of the next. Each molecule holds a few neighbours like this, again and again, all through the water. Scientists call these hydrogen bonds. They are why a drop is round, and why a water strider can walk on a pond. They are also why a thread of water in a tree can be pulled up without snapping.
examples: A paperclip laid gently on still water can float, held up by the water's skin.
Fill a steel tumbler to the brim, then add drops one by one. The water bulges above the rim before it spills.
Water creeps up a tissue because it clings to the paper and to itself.
explanations.art: A zoom into a water drop: many small molecules, each a big ball with two small balls, the small ball of one tugging the big ball of the next with little dotted lines.
explanations.context: Why does a thread of water not snap as it is pulled up a tree? This card zooms in to the tiny bits that water is made of.

explanations.definition: The energy that lifts water up a plant comes from the Sun. Sunlight warms the leaves and makes water evaporate. The plant does not spend their own food energy to lift the water.
explanations.description: Lifting water is work. Ask anyone who has carried a bucket up the stairs. Your heart uses energy from your food every second to push your blood round. A tree has no heart. Instead, sunlight warms the wet inside of each leaf, and water evaporates out of the holes. Turning water into vapour takes a lot of energy, and most of it comes from sunlight. The plant does not spend their own food on the lift. Evaporation also cools the leaves, the way sweat drying on your skin cools you. That is part of why the shade of a big tree feels so cool.
examples: Sweat drying on your arm cools you. Water leaving a leaf cools the leaf.
On a hot day, the air under a big neem or banyan tree feels cooler than the air in a car park.
explanations.art: A big Sun sending golden rays into a leaf. Inside the leaf, water drops turning into vapour and flying out, and a thread of water rising up the stem below.
explanations.context: Something must do the hard work of lifting water up a tree. This card explains that the power comes from the Sun.

explanations.concept: Why a straw cannot do what a tree does
explanations.definition: When you suck on a straw, the air pushing on the drink outside pushes it up the straw. That push can only lift water about 10 metres, even with a perfect pump. Tall trees lift water much higher, so they must work in a different way.
explanations.description: Sucking does not really pull the drink. It takes air out of the straw. Then the air pressing on the drink in the glass pushes it up into the straw. But the air can only push water up about 10 metres, the height of a three-storey building. No suction pump can lift water higher than that. Yet the tallest tree alive, a coast redwood called Hyperion in California, is about 116 metres tall. Their water threads are not pushed up by air. They are pulled from the top and hang together by cohesion, like a rope being pulled up a well. Scientists say the water in a tall tree is under tension, a stretching pull.
examples: A simple hand pump at the top of a well can lift water from only about 7 or 8 metres down. Deeper wells need a pump down at the water.
A coconut palm can be 25 metres tall. That is already more than twice the straw limit.
explanations.art: A side-by-side picture: a giant straw reaching 10 metres up a building, with water stopping at the 10 metre mark, next to a towering redwood with water reaching the top.
explanations.context: Is a tree like a giant drinking straw? This card shows why it cannot be, using the height limit for sucking.

explanations.concept: Bubbles in the tubes, and plants that click
explanations.description: The water threads in a tree are stretched tight. If the plant gets very thirsty, a thread can snap and a tiny air bubble can form in the tube. Scientists call this an embolism. A tube with a bubble cannot carry water. Flower sellers know about this. They cut flower stems again under water, so no air gets into the fresh tube ends. Snapping threads also make tiny clicks. In 1966, John Milburn and Robert Johnson listened to thirsty castor plants with sensitive sound detectors and heard the clicks. In 2023, a team at Tel Aviv University in Israel, led by Lilach Hadany, recorded thirsty tomato and tobacco plants clicking. The sounds were too high for people to hear. The team recorded them with microphones 10 centimetres from the plants.
examples: Cut roses last longer when their stems are trimmed under water.
A thirsty tomato plant in the Tel Aviv study clicked dozens of times an hour. A well-watered one hardly clicked at all.

perspectives.explanation: The clicks most likely come from water threads snapping and bubbles forming in thirsty tubes.
Moths, mice or other plants might be able to hear these clicks and learn that a plant is thirsty. Nobody has shown this yet.
The clicks are most likely a side effect of bubbles forming, like the creak of a floor, and not a message. The question is still open.

explanations.art: A thirsty tomato plant in a pot with a tiny microphone near their stem, little sound waves coming out, and a magnified tube inside with an air bubble.
explanations.context: What happens when a thirsty plant's water threads snap? This card is about air bubbles in the tubes, and a recent surprise: plants that click.

explanations.description: The first plants on land were small and flat, like mosses today. They had no stiff, strong water tubes. So they had to stay low, close to damp ground, and soak water up through their whole body. Fossils show that by about 430 million years ago some small plants had simple water tubes. Later, plants used a tough material called lignin to make their tubes and stems stiff. Lignin is what makes wood hard. With strong pipes, plants could grow upwards and reach the light above their neighbours. By about 385 million years ago, the first forests of tall trees had grown. Scientists agree on this broad story from the fossils. The exact dates and order keep changing as new fossils are found.
examples: Moss on a wall in the monsoon grows only a few centimetres tall.
A fern has water tubes, and grows much taller than moss.
A banyan tree's hanging roots grow down to the soil and become new pillars that carry water too.
explanations.art: A timeline strip: flat moss on wet rock, a small stick-like early plant with a tube drawn inside, a fern, and then a tall ancient forest.
explanations.context: Why are mosses tiny and trees huge? This card is about how water tubes let plants grow tall, hundreds of millions of years ago.

explanations.description: All the water leaving leaves goes up into the air. Over a forest, it can form clouds and fall again as rain, further along. Scientists have measured this in the Amazon rainforest in South America. The forest sends so much water into the air that some call it a flying river. Plants are a big part of the water cycle. That is the endless trip of water from land and sea, up to the sky, and back. But how big a part? Scientists still argue about that.
examples: A big tree on a hot day can send hundreds of litres of water into the air.
Cutting down large forests can make the land around them drier.

perspectives.who: Scott Jasechko and colleagues, in the journal Nature, 2013
perspectives.explanation: They estimated that plants send up most of the water that rises from land: about 80 to 90 out of every 100 drops. The rest evaporates from soil, lakes and rivers.

perspectives.who: William Schlesinger and Scott Jasechko, in 2014, after comparing many studies
perspectives.explanation: After more studies, they gave a lower estimate: about 60 out of every 100 drops. Different methods give different answers.
Plants send a very large share of the land's water back into the sky. The exact amount is still being measured.

explanations.art: A green forest with mist rising from the treetops, forming a long cloud river that rains down on farms further away.
explanations.context: What happens to all the water that leaves leaves? This card follows it into the sky, and into an argument about how much rain plants make.

chart.title: Of 100 drops of water rising from land, how many come from plants? (one 2014 estimate)

data.label: From soil, lakes and rivers: about 40

explanations.concept: How tall can a tree grow?
explanations.description: The higher water has to climb, the harder the pull on the thread. And the harder the pull, the more likely the thread is to snap. In 2004, George Koch and his team climbed the tallest redwood trees in California and studied their top leaves. The top leaves were small and thirsty, as if the water barely reached them. From this they estimated that no redwood could grow much taller than about 122 to 130 metres. The tallest known tree, Hyperion, is about 116 metres. Other scientists think other limits, like wind and getting enough food to the top, also matter. Nobody knows for sure.
examples: The tallest kinds of tree, coast redwoods and mountain ash trees from Australia, can grow taller than 90 metres.
A redwood's top leaves are much smaller than their lower leaves.
explanations.art: A giant redwood next to a tall building for scale, with a dotted line above the treetop labelled 'the limit?' and a scientist on a rope near the top.
explanations.context: Could a tree grow as tall as a mountain? This card is about the limit that water sets on how tall trees can grow.

explanations.concept: Plants and bodies: a pull, not a pump
explanations.definition: Your blood is pushed round your body in a loop by your heart. A plant's water goes one way, from root to leaf, pulled from the top by evaporation. Most of the water tubes are dead cells.
explanations.description: You and a plant both need to move water to every part. Your body uses a living pump, your heart, and living pipes, your blood vessels. The blood goes round and round. A plant uses dead, hollow tubes, and the pull of water evaporating in the Sun. The water goes one way only, up and out. A plant does have a second set of living tubes, the phloem, that carry sugary food both up and down. Both of you cool off in the same way, though. You sweat. A leaf lets water evaporate.
examples: When you run, your heart beats faster to push more blood. On a hot day, a plant pulls more water.
Blood keeps going round your body. Water leaves the plant and goes into the sky.
explanations.art: Two outlines side by side: a child with a red heart and a loop of blood vessels, and a tree with blue upward arrows and mist leaving the leaves.
explanations.context: How is a plant moving water like your body moving blood? This card compares the two, and finds one big difference.

explanations.concept: Plants in space, and the water's long journey
explanations.definition: In space, water does not drip downwards. So astronauts on the International Space Station grow plants in soft pillows with wicks. The wicks feed water to the roots by capillary action.
explanations.description: On Earth, gravity pulls water down into the soil and around the roots. On the space station, everything floats. Water clumps into wobbly balls and can drown roots or float away. NASA's Veggie garden grows lettuce in small pillows of soil that soak up water through wicks, like a cotton thread. The water in your plant also has a very long story. Its hydrogen was made soon after the universe began, about 13.8 billion years ago. Its oxygen atoms were made inside stars that exploded long before the Sun was born. The same water has been through clouds, seas, dinosaurs and trees, over and over.
examples: Astronauts on the space station have grown and eaten lettuce they grew there.
The water in your glass may once have been inside a dinosaur or a tree in an ancient forest.
explanations.art: An astronaut floating beside small pillows with lettuce growing from them, wicks drawing water in. In the corner, a star exploding and a drop of water.
explanations.context: This card goes far out: how plants drink in space, and where the water in a plant first came from.

agreed.text: Water travels into a plant through the roots. It goes up the stem in tiny tubes called xylem, and out to the leaves and flowers.
agreed.evidence: Stand a white flower in coloured water. The colour reaches the petals, and a cut stem shows coloured dots where the tubes are. Scientists also see the tubes under microscopes.

agreed.text: Most of the water a plant takes up leaves through tiny holes in their leaves, as vapour.
agreed.evidence: A bag tied over a leafy branch fills with mist and drops. Stephen Hales weighed potted plants in 1727 and found they lost a lot of water each day. Plant scientists estimate that more than 90 out of every 100 drops a plant takes up go back into the air.

chart.title: Of every 100 drops a plant takes up, where do they go? (a rough estimate, it varies)

data.label: Out of the leaves into the air: about 97
Kept or used to make food: about 3

agreed.text: Water is pulled up from the top, as it evaporates from the leaves. Water molecules hold together in unbroken threads as they rise.
agreed.evidence: Dixon and Joly proposed this in 1894. Since then, scientists have measured the stretching pull inside the water tubes of many plants. Leafy stems pull water up faster than bare ones.

agreed.text: A plant wilts when they lose water faster than they can take it in.
agreed.evidence: A wilted plant given water stands up again within hours. Plants droop most on hot, dry afternoons.

agreed.text: Sun, warmth, wind and dry air make plants lose water faster.
agreed.evidence: In the Sweating Branch test, the branch in the sun gives off more water than the one in the shade. Gardeners see it every summer: plants in hot sun and wind need watering more often.

challenging.claim: Plants drink mainly through their leaves, so we should pour water over the leaves.
challenging.who: A common idea, especially when people water plants from above
challenging.for: Leaves do get wet in the rain, and a very little water can soak in through leaves.
challenging.against: Almost all the water a plant uses comes in through their roots. Water poured on the leaves mostly runs off or evaporates. Leaves that stay wet overnight can even help some plant diseases spread. Water the soil, near the roots.
challenging.context: This card is about a common habit when watering plants, and whether it really helps the plant drink.

challenging.claim: Living cells in the stem pump water up, like tiny hearts.
challenging.who: Jagadish Chandra Bose, the great Indian scientist, in 1923
challenging.for: Bose's very sensitive instruments recorded tiny rhythmic electrical pulses in the living cells of stems. He believed these pulses were the pump.
challenging.against: In 1891, Eduard Strasburger killed the living cells in long stems, and liquid still climbed up them. The main water tubes are dead cells anyway. Today almost all plant scientists accept the pulling idea of Dixon and Joly instead. Bose was wrong about this, but right about many other things, like plants sensing touch and injury.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous idea from Jagadish Chandra Bose, an Indian scientist, about how water climbs up plants.

challenging.claim: The roots push water all the way to the top of a tree.
challenging.who: An early idea, from the work of Stephen Hales and others
challenging.for: Roots really do push. A cut vine drips sap, and beads of water appear on grass tips in the morning.
challenging.against: Root pressure is small. It can push water up a few metres, and many trees show none at all in summer, when they need the most water. It cannot lift water 100 metres up a redwood. The pull from the leaves does most of the work.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that roots push water up a plant, and why it cannot explain tall trees.

challenging.claim: Water climbs a stem the way tea climbs a tissue, by capillary action alone.
challenging.who: Many children, and some older books
challenging.for: Water does creep up thin gaps by itself, and plant tubes are very thin.
challenging.against: Capillary action alone can only lift water a short way in tubes as wide as a plant's, much less than the height of a tall tree. It helps water cling to the tube walls, but the big lift comes from the pull of evaporation at the leaves.
challenging.context: Tea climbs up a tissue dipped in it. This card asks whether that is how water climbs a tree.

challenging.claim: Plants waste water by letting most of it escape from their leaves.
challenging.who: A common way of seeing it, especially in dry places
challenging.for: Most of the water a plant takes up does go straight back into the air.
challenging.against: The plant must open their leaf holes to let in air for making food, and water escapes whenever they are open. The escaping water also cools the leaves, pulls minerals up from the soil, and returns water to the sky as rain. Scientists see it as a price the plant pays, not a waste.
challenging.context: Most of the water a plant drinks escapes into the air. This card asks whether that is a waste.

challenging.claim: Thirsty plants click, and animals or other plants can hear it and learn something.
challenging.who: Lilach Hadany's team in Tel Aviv, as an idea to test, after their 2023 study
challenging.for: The clicks are real and were recorded from about 10 centimetres away. Some moths and mice hear sounds this high.
challenging.against: Nobody has yet shown any animal or plant listening to these clicks or acting on them. They may just be a side effect of air bubbles forming.
challenging.context: In 2023, scientists recorded thirsty plants making tiny clicks. This card asks whether anything is listening.

big_questions.q: A tree has no heart and no pump. How can they lift water higher than a house, every single day?
big_questions.hint: Think about the line of children holding hands up the stairs. Who is doing the pulling?

big_questions.q: Why does a thread of water not snap when it is pulled up a tall tree?
big_questions.hint: Try floating a paperclip on water, or filling a tumbler until the water bulges over the top.

big_questions.q: The water in your glass may once have been inside a dinosaur, a cloud and a mango tree. Who does water really belong to?
big_questions.hint: Where was this water last week? Where will it be next year?

big_questions.q: A plant lets almost all of their water go into the air. What would happen to the plant, and to the rain, if they kept it all?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the open leaf holes let in, what the escaping water does for the leaf, and where the vapour goes.

big_questions.q: Jagadish Chandra Bose was one of India's greatest scientists, and he was wrong about how water climbs. Can a great scientist be wrong? Does that make them less great?
big_questions.hint: What did other scientists do with his idea? How do we find out who is right?

big_questions.q: You cannot see water climbing inside a stem. So how can you be sure it does?
big_questions.hint: What did the coloured water show you? What is evidence?

big_questions.q: Thirsty plants make clicks too high for us to hear. What else might be happening around us that our senses miss?
big_questions.hint: Think of sounds dogs hear, colours bees see, and smells ants follow.

big_questions.q: If all the trees in a forest are cut, the rain can change far away. Who should decide whether a forest is cut?
big_questions.hint: Think of the farmers who live where the rain falls, and the people who want the wood.

big_questions.q: Why can moss grow only a few centimetres tall, while a tree can grow taller than a 30-storey building?
big_questions.hint: What does a tree have inside that moss does not?

big_questions.q: Your heart uses energy from your food to push your blood. A tree uses the Sun's heat to lift their water. Where did the energy in your food come from in the first place?
big_questions.hint: Think about where rice, dal and fruit come from, and what plants need to grow.

big_questions.q: A banyan tree can live for hundreds of years, drinking every day. How many buckets of water do you think they have lifted in their life?
big_questions.hint: Think of hundreds of litres a day, for every day of hundreds of years.

story.title: Blue Before Morning
story.note: Mullick Ghat flower market under Howrah Bridge in Kolkata is real. Florists in many countries colour white flowers by standing their stems in coloured water. Cutting stems again under water is a real florists' trick to keep air out of the tubes. Rumki, her mother, Rahima Khala and the wedding order are made up.
text: Under the great iron bridge in Kolkata, where the river slides past brown and slow, there is a flower market that never sleeps. Marigolds lie in orange hills. Roses come in wet sacks. And at the far end, where the steps go down to the water, Rumki's mother had a stall no wider than a bed.
Rumki was ten. She could tie a marigold garland faster than she could say her eight times table. But on the evening of this story, there was no time for garlands.

A man in a shiny shirt had come to the stall. 'My daughter is getting married tomorrow,' he said. 'She wants blue flowers. Blue like the sky over her grandmother's village. Three hundred stems of rajnigandha, blue, by six in the morning.' He put down more money than Rumki had ever seen her mother hold. 'Can you do it?'
Rajnigandha is white. Their flowers are small and waxy and smell of night. Nobody grows a blue one.
'I can do it,' said Rumki's mother.
Rumki stared at her. Her mother only winked.

That evening they bought three hundred stems from a farmer whose cart had stood in the sun all afternoon. The stems were a little tired. Then Rumki ran to Bhola-da's sweet shop and came back with four small bottles of blue food colour, the kind he used for his sugar birds. They filled two plastic buckets with water, poured in the colour until it was dark as ink, and stood the stems inside. Then they carried the buckets into the little back room behind the stall, where it was warm and quiet, and shut the door so that nobody would knock them over.
'Now the flowers will drink,' said her mother. 'By morning, they will drink the blue right up into their petals.'
Rumki fell asleep on a pile of empty sacks.
When she woke, it was midnight. The market was humming. Her mother was holding a lantern over the buckets, and she looked worried.
The flowers were white. Not a single petal had a speck of blue.
'They are not drinking,' her mother whispered. 'I have done this a hundred times. Why aren't they drinking?'

Rumki looked at the stems standing in the dark blue water. They looked as if they were waiting for something. She thought of the farmer's cart, and the stems lying in a heap in the hot afternoon sun, their cut ends open to the air.
And she thought of Rahima Khala.

Rahima Khala had the stall next to theirs. She made the long white garlands for weddings, and she was very old and very slow, and she did one thing that had always made Rumki laugh. Before she put any flower into water, she held its stem under the water in her big tin tub. Then she cut the end off, there, under the water, with her little curved knife. Never in the air. Always under the water.
'Why do you do that, Khala?' she had asked her once.

'So the stem doesn't swallow air,' she had said. 'A stem is a bundle of tiny pipes, beti, finer than your hair. Inside each pipe is one long thread of water, all the way up to the flower. If air gets in at the bottom, the thread breaks. Then the flower can pull and pull, and nothing comes.'
Rumki had thought Khala was telling her a story. Now she looked at the white flowers, and her heart started to race.
'Ma,' she said. 'Bring the knife.'

So that is what they did, in the middle of the night. Rumki held each stem down under the blue water, and her mother cut a finger's width off the bottom with the kitchen knife. Snip, under the water. Three hundred times. Their arms went blue to the elbow.

But when they had finished, the room was still hot and still, and the air was thick and wet, like the inside of a cooking pot with the lid on. Rumki thought of the washing on the roof. Her mother always said clothes dried fastest in the wind off the river, and slowest on a still, wet day. If the flowers had to let water go, to pull more water up behind it, then they needed somewhere to let it go to.
'The roof,' she said. 'Ma, they need the wind.'

They carried the heavy buckets up the narrow stairs, one by one, slopping blue onto the steps. On the roof, the river wind came off the water, cool and steady, and it moved through the white flowers like a hand through hair. Rumki sat beside the buckets with her knees under her chin. She watched the lights of the bridge. She did not sleep.

At about four o'clock, when the sky was the colour of a pigeon's wing, she saw it. At the very edge of one petal, a thin blue line, as fine as a thread. Then another. Then, as she looked closer, she saw that each petal had tiny blue roads running through it, branching and branching, like the map of a city. The blue was climbing the pipes. It was following the water to the place where the water left, into the wind.
By six o'clock, three hundred rajnigandha stood in the buckets, white at the centre, blue at every edge and every vein, as if someone had drawn them with a pen made of sky.

The man in the shiny shirt came. He looked at the flowers for a long time and said nothing. Then he paid, and he gave Rumki an extra ten rupees, and he carried the buckets to his car very carefully, the way people carry babies.
When he had gone, Rahima Khala shuffled over to look at the blue drips on the stairs. 'Under the water?' she asked.
'Under the water,' said Rumki. 'And then the wind.'
The old woman nodded, as if this was the most ordinary thing in the world. Then she went back to her tub, held a stem under the water, and cut.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the flowers do not take up the colour just because they are standing in it. They take it up because water evaporates from the petals and leaves, and that pulls more water up the stem. Two things stopped that pull in the story. Air got into the cut ends while the stems lay in the sun, and broke the threads of water in the tubes. And the hot, still, damp back room gave the water nowhere to evaporate. Cutting off the ends under water gives each tube a fresh end full of water. The river wind lets the water evaporate. Then the blue climbs, and shows the tubes inside every petal. The story also notices the quiet expert at the next stall, whose habit everyone laughed at.
ask: The flowers stood in blue water for hours and stayed white. Why do you think they were not drinking?
Why did Rahima Khala always cut stems under the water, never in the air?
Why did Rumki carry the buckets up to the windy roof?
What did the thin blue lines in the petals show Rumki?
Rumki's mother had coloured flowers a hundred times. What was different about these stems?

rules: Each player is a drop of water. Put your drop on square 1, in the soil.
On your turn, roll a dice and move that many squares.
Whenever you land on a square with a star, take a card and do what it says.
Read the name of each part out loud as you pass into it: soil, root hairs, root, stem, veins, leaf hole, air, rain.
The first drop to fall back into the soil as rain, on square 30, wins.
After the game, everyone tells the whole journey of their drop in their own words.

flow.do: 1. Lay the board on the floor. 2. Shuffle the cards and put them face down. 3. Give each player a drop counter on square 1.
flow.say: Each of us is a drop of water in the soil, under a plant. Let's race up through the plant, out into the sky, and back down as rain.
flow.kid: You are a drop of water in the soil. Put your drop on square 1. Race through the plant to the sky!
flow.context: This is the first step of Drop's Journey. It is a board game. Each player is a drop of water travelling through a plant, from soil to leaf to sky.

flow.do: Before rolling, trace the whole path on the board together with one finger, saying each part's name.
flow.say: First, let's trace the road. Soil. Root hairs. Root. Stem. Veins. Leaf hole. Air. Rain. Which part comes straight after the root?
flow.kid: Trace the road with your finger. Say each part. Soil, root hairs, root, stem, veins, leaf hole, air, rain.

check.q: In Drop's Journey, which part does the drop reach straight after the root?
options: The leaf
The stem
The flower
check.why: Water goes from the roots into the stem, and climbs the stem's tubes before it reaches any leaf or flower. Picking the leaf usually means skipping the stem, as if water jumped straight from root to leaf.

flow.do: 1. Take turns rolling and moving. 2. When someone lands on a star, they read a card out loud. 3. Before they move, ask them to say why the card makes sense.
flow.say: You got 'Hot sunny afternoon, move ahead 3'. Why would a hot sun make a drop move faster?
flow.kid: Roll and move. Landed on a star? Take a card and read it. Say why it makes sense. Then move.

ask.q: Why does the air bubble card send you back?
good: The bubble breaks the thread of water, so it can't be pulled up.
A tube with air in it can't carry water.

ask.q: Why does night make you miss a turn?
good: The leaf holes close at night.
Less water leaves the leaves when it is dark and cool.

flow.parent: Good reasons: sun, warmth, wind and dry air make leaves lose water faster, and that pulls water up faster. Night, mist and closed leaf holes slow it down. Torn root hairs mean the plant cannot drink.

flow.do: When the game ends, each player tells the full journey of their drop, in order, without looking at the board.
flow.say: Tell me your drop's whole journey, from the soil to the sky and back. What happened on the way?
flow.kid: Tell the story of your drop. Where did it start? Where did it go? How did it get back to the soil?
flow.think: The drop went back into the soil as rain. Could it go through the same plant again? Could it go through you?

games.context: This is a board game about the journey of a drop of water. It goes into a plant's roots and up the stem. Then it goes out through a leaf into the sky, and back down as rain.

rules: Each leaf player puts their two hands together, palms touching. The hands are the two guard cells around a leaf hole.
Open the hole by bending your hands apart into a round shape. Close it by pressing them together.
The caller reads a card. Each leaf decides fast: open or close? Show it with your hands.

flow.do: Show your child how to make a leaf hole with two hands. Bend the hands apart to open, press them together to close.
flow.say: Every leaf has thousands of tiny holes. Each one has two curved cells around it, like your two hands. They open the hole or close it.
flow.kid: Put your hands together. They are two guard cells. Bend them apart to open the hole. Press them together to close it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Open or Close?. In this game, your two hands are the guard cells around a tiny leaf hole. They open and close to let air in and water out.

flow.do: Play the first card together as practice: 'Hot afternoon, soil is very dry'.
flow.say: Hot afternoon, and the soil is very dry. Open or close? Think about the water.
flow.kid: Practice card: hot afternoon, very dry soil. Open or close? Show your hands.

check.q: Hot afternoon, and the soil is very dry. What do the leaf holes usually do?
options: Open wide to cool down
Close, to save water
Nothing changes
check.why: When the soil is dry, the roots cannot replace the water fast enough. If the holes stayed open, the plant would wilt or even dry out. So most plants close their holes, even though this stops air coming in. Picking 'open wide to cool down' is a good thought, because evaporation does cool a leaf. But a plant with no water to spare must save it first.

flow.do: 1. Play the rest of the cards. 2. After each one, ask a leaf to say why. 3. Give a point for any reason that mentions water or air.
flow.say: Bright morning sun, soil is wet. Open or close? Why?
flow.kid: Listen to each card. Open or close? Show your hands fast. Then say why.
flow.parent: Usual answers: open in bright light with wet soil. The leaf needs air to make food, and has water to spare. Close at night, because there is no light to make food. Close in a heatwave or drought, to save water. A cactus closes in the day and opens at night, when it is cooler and less water escapes. A plant in a bag full of damp air can stay open, because little water leaves into air that is already wet. Torn roots: close, because the plant cannot replace lost water. Rice in a wet field: open, because they have plenty of water. A cut flower in a vase in the light: open, because they can still drink from the vase.

flow.do: Talk about the hardest card.
flow.say: Which card was hardest to decide? Why is it hard for a plant to choose?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? Why is it hard for a plant to choose?
flow.think: If a plant kept their leaf holes shut all day, they would save water. What would they go without?
