items.p: Put the path of water through a plant in order, from start to end: stem, air, root hairs, leaf, root.
items: root hairs
root
stem
leaf
air
items.a: order shown
items.why: Root hairs soak up the water, and it moves into the root. It climbs the stem and spreads through the leaf. Then it leaves into the air as vapour.

items.p: Each root hair is thinner than a sewing thread. Why does a root have thousands of root hairs, not a few thick roots?
opts: Thousands of thin hairs touch much more soil, so they soak up more water
Thin hairs are stronger than thick roots
Root hairs catch light under the soil
items.why: Water gets in wherever a root touches wet soil. Thousands of thin hairs squeeze between the soil grains and touch far more soil than a few fat roots could. Picking 'stronger' mixes up the job of soaking with the job of holding on.

items.p: If you pull a seedling out roughly and plant them again, they may wilt, even though their main roots are still there.
items.why: True. Pulling roughly tears off the tiny root hairs, and the root hairs do most of the soaking. Until new hairs grow, the seedling cannot drink enough. That is why gardeners move seedlings with a ball of soil round their roots.

items.p: A white flower stood in blue water for a day. Then its petals had blue edges. What does this show?
opts: Water travelled up the stem into the petals
The blue soaked through the air
items.why: The colour can only reach the petals by travelling with the water, up the stem. Picking 'soaked through the air' usually means not noticing that the petals never touched the blue water.
items.context: In the Blue Climb experiment, you stand a pale leaf or a white flower in coloured water. Then you watch where the colour goes.

items.p: Most of the water a plant takes in leaves again through tiny holes in their leaves.
items.why: True. More than 90 out of every 100 drops go back into the air as vapour. This is called transpiration.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, says, 'Plants are wasteful. They let most of their water escape into the air.' What would you tell her?
items.a: I would tell her the escaping water is not wasted. As water leaves the leaves, it pulls more water up the stem, and that water brings minerals up from the soil. The escaping water also cools the leaves. And the holes must be open to let air in, so the leaf can make food.
items.why: A strong answer says what transpiration does for the plant: it pulls water and minerals up, and cools the leaves. Losing water is the cost of keeping the holes open for air.

items.p: In the Sweating Branch test, which bag collected more water?
items.why: Sun warms the leaves and they let out more water vapour, which turns back into drops on the bag. Picking 'the shade' usually means thinking cool places are wetter. But these drops came out of the plant.
items.context: In the Sweating Branch test, you tie clear bags over two leafy branches. One is in the sun and one is in the shade. The bags catch the water the leaves let out.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: soaks up water from the soil
a tiny hole in a leaf
a line on a leaf that holds water tubes
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Root hairs soak water in, xylem carries it up, veins spread it through the leaf, and stomata let it out.

items.p: A balsam plant is drooping on a hot afternoon. What is most likely happening?
opts: They are losing water from their leaves faster than their roots can drink
items.why: Wilting means the plant is losing water faster than they can take it in, so their cells go soft. Picking 'sleeping' is a fun idea. Some plants do fold their leaves at night, but that is different from wilting in the heat.

items.p: Sort these. Do they make a plant lose water FASTER or SLOWER?
items: hot sun
Faster
a cool night
Slower
a strong dry wind
Faster
a damp misty morning
Slower
lots of leaves
Faster
the leaf holes closed
Slower
items.a: see items
items.why: Sun, warmth, wind, dry air and many leaves all speed up water loss. Cool, still, damp air and closed holes slow it down. It is like drying clothes.

items.p: Hold a leaf up to the light. You see a net of veins reaching every corner. Why does a leaf need veins everywhere?
opts: So every part of the leaf gets water
To make the leaf look pretty
items.why: The water tubes run inside the veins. A part of the leaf with no vein nearby would dry out and could not make food. Veins also stiffen the leaf, like the ribs of an umbrella. Picking 'to keep the leaf green' mixes up veins with chlorophyll.

items.p: A plant that has wilted and gone floppy is dead.
items.why: False. A wilted plant has lost water, so their cells have gone soft. Give them water in time and the cells fill up and go firm again. In Bring Back the Wilted Coriander, a floppy bunch stood in water and became crisp within an hour. Only a plant left dry for too long dies.
items.context: In Bring Back the Wilted Coriander, you stand a floppy bunch of coriander in water and watch.

items.p: Tell the story of one drop of water, from the soil to the sky. Use the words root, stem and leaf.
items.a: My drop was in the wet soil. A root hair soaked it up into the root. It climbed up the stem through a tiny tube. It went along a vein in a leaf. Then it went out of a tiny hole and floated into the air as vapour.
items.why: A full answer has the parts in the right order: root, stem, leaf, air.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Class 3, says, 'I water my plant by spraying the leaves.' What would you tell her, and why?
items.a: I would tell her to water the soil, near the roots. Plants drink mostly through their roots, not their leaves. Most of the water on the leaves just runs off or dries away.
items.why: Any answer that says to water the soil, because roots do the drinking, is right.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 4, and her family in Madurai water the tulsi pot once a day. They disagree about the best time.

views.says: Water early in the morning. Then the plant has plenty to drink before the hot sun makes their leaves lose water fast.
Water in the evening. The Sun has gone, so less water dries off the soil, and the roots have all night to drink.

items.ask: Whose plan would you follow? Give a reason from what you learned about when plants lose water fastest. Then say what the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the science. For the morning: leaves lose water fastest in hot sun and wind, so the plant needs water ready before the hot part of the day. For the evening: the soil loses less water to the air when it is cool, so more of it stays for the roots. A strong answer then admits the other side's point. Many gardeners say both work, as long as the soil is watered, not the leaves.
items.why: Both are real gardeners' habits, and each has a good reason. What makes an answer strong is linking the time of day to how fast water leaves the plant and the soil.

items.p: Draw a plant in a pot. Draw blue arrows to show the path of water from the soil to the air. Label root, stem, leaf and air.
items.a: Arrows start in the soil, go into the roots, up the stem, along the leaves, and out of the leaves into the air.
items.why: The arrows should go one way, upwards, and end in the air.
items.art: An outline of a potted plant for the child to draw arrows on.

items.p: After the Blue Climb, a grown-up cuts across the flower's stem. Draw what you see at the cut end. Label the coloured dots and say what each dot is.
items.a: A circle for the cut stem with a ring of coloured dots near the edge. A label says each dot is a bundle of xylem tubes that the coloured water climbed through.
items.why: The colour shows as dots, not all over, because the water travels only inside the tubes. Each dot is one bundle of tubes.
items.context: In the Blue Climb experiment, you stand a pale leaf or a white flower in coloured water. Then you watch where the colour goes.

items.p: In the Leafy or Bare test, why did we pour a thin layer of oil on the water?
opts: So water could not evaporate from the bottle itself
items.why: The oil is a lid. Then any water that disappears must have gone up the stem. Picking 'to feed the stems' means thinking plants eat what is in their water.
items.context: In the Leafy or Bare test, two stems stand in two bottles of water with oil on top. One stem has leaves and one has none. You measure how far each water level drops.

items.p: In the Leafy or Bare test, the leafy stem's water dropped 18 mm and the bare stem's dropped 3 mm. How many times more did the leafy stem drink?
items.why: 18 divided by 3 is 6. So the leafy stem drank 6 times as much. Picking 15 means taking away instead of dividing. 18 take away 3 is 15 mm more, which is also true, but it does not say how many times.
items.context: In the Leafy or Bare test, two stems stand in two bottles of water with oil on top. One stem has leaves and one has none. You measure how far each water level drops.

chart.title: Made-up example: water level drop in 2 days

items.p: Fill a steel tumbler to the brim. Then add a few more drops, gently. The water bulges above the rim without spilling. Which idea from this unit does this show?
opts: Water molecules hold on to each other
Water is lighter at the top
items.why: The water at the top holds on to the water around it, so it bulges instead of spilling. This holding on is called cohesion. It is the same pull that keeps a thread of water in a tree from snapping. Picking 'leaves pull water up' names a true idea, but there are no leaves here.

items.p: Plants need minerals, tiny bits from the soil like nitrogen, to grow. The minerals are dissolved in the soil water. How do they reach the leaves?
opts: They travel up with the water in the xylem tubes
The leaves catch them from the air
items.why: Dissolved minerals ride along with the water, like sugar dissolved in tea. When water is pulled up the xylem, the minerals come too. Picking 'from the air' mixes up minerals with the carbon dioxide that leaves take in.

items.p: A grown-up splits the bottom of a white flower's stem into two halves. One half stands in blue water and the other in red. Predict what the flower will look like the next day, and explain why.
items.a: One side of the flower will go blue and the other side red. Each half of the stem has its own tubes, and each tube carries water to its own part of the flower. The tubes do not mix, so the colours stay apart.
items.why: A strong answer makes a clear guess and gives the reason: the stem is a bundle of separate tubes. Many people first guess purple, because the stem looks like one pipe.
items.context: In the Two-Colour Flower activity, a grown-up splits the bottom of a white flower's stem into two halves. Each half stands in a different colour.

items.p: Match each person to their idea about how water climbs.
pairs: weighed plants and showed leaves lose lots of water
showed water climbs even when stem cells are killed
water is pulled up from the top and holds together
living cells pump water up, like tiny hearts
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four scientists each added a piece to the puzzle. Today, the pulling idea of Dixon and Joly is accepted.

items.p: Is the water drop from INSIDE the plant or from the AIR?
items: one round drop at the tip of a grass blade at dawn
From inside the plant
tiny drops all over a leaf on a cold morning
From the air
drops inside a bag tied over a branch
From inside the plant
drops on the outside of a cold steel tumbler
From the air
items.a: see items
items.why: Drops at grass tips are pushed out by the roots, and drops in the bag came out of the leaves. Dew and drops on a cold tumbler form from water vapour in the air.

items.p: Water creeping up a paper towel or a thin cloth wick is called ____ action.
items.why: In capillary action, water clings to the thin fibres and to itself, so it creeps up the narrow gaps. It lifts water only a few centimetres, far less than a tree does.

items.p: In the Water Chain play, one person in the middle let go of hands. Why did the people below them stop moving up?
opts: Nothing was pulling them any more, like a broken thread of water
items.why: The pull from the top only travels along joined hands. An air bubble breaks a real water thread in the same way. Picking 'the roots stopped pushing' means thinking roots do the main work.
items.context: In the Water Chain play, people hold hands up a staircase. They act out water being pulled up a tube in a plant.

items.p: Mosses stay small partly because they have no stiff, strong water tubes like a tree's.
items.why: True. Without strong tubes to carry water up, mosses stay low, close to damp ground.

items.p: In Be Stephen Hales, you wrap the pot and soil in a plastic bag before you weigh the plant each day. Why?
opts: So water can leave only through the leaves, and the weight loss shows what the leaves let out
To stop insects eating the soil
items.why: Water can dry off wet soil too. With the soil sealed, any weight the plant loses must be water that went out through the leaves. Stephen Hales did this in the 1720s. Picking 'keep the plant warm' misses that the bag is there to make the test fair.
items.context: In the Be Stephen Hales project, you cover a pot's soil so water can only leave through the leaves. Then you weigh the plant every day.

items.p: A cut flower in a vase has no roots at all. Yet the water in the vase goes down day by day. How does the flower drink without roots?
items.a: The water is pulled up from the top. Water evaporates from the leaves and petals, and the water in the tubes is pulled up behind it, because water molecules hold on to each other. Roots are not needed for this pull.
items.why: This tests the common idea that roots pump water up. A strong answer says the pull comes from water leaving the top, which a cut stem can still do.

items.p: It is a hot, dry afternoon. Two friends, Meenakshi and Farhan, argue about what a mango leaf should do with their tiny leaf holes, the stomata.

views.says: Keep the holes open. The leaf needs air to come in to make food, and the water leaving cools the leaf down.
Close the holes. In this heat the plant is losing water faster than the roots can drink, and they will wilt.

items.ask: Whose side are you on? Use what you know about stomata. Then say what the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees the trade-off. Open holes let in the carbon dioxide the leaf needs to make food, and the evaporating water cools the leaf. But open holes also let water escape, and a plant short of water can wilt. Many plants close their holes in the hottest, driest part of the day and open them again when it is cooler. A strong answer gives the other friend's point too.
items.why: Both friends are partly right. A plant cannot get air in without letting water out. Plants manage this by opening and closing their stomata as the day changes.

items.p: Imagine a plant with no leaves at all. Would water still climb up their stem? Explain using the Leafy or Bare test.
items.a: Only a little. In the Leafy or Bare test, the bare stem drank only 3 mm, but the leafy stem drank 18 mm. Without leaves, there is almost nowhere for the water to leave, so almost nothing pulls it up.
items.why: A good answer uses the evidence from the test and says the leaves do the pulling.
items.context: In the Leafy or Bare test, two stems stand in two bottles of water with oil on top. One stem has leaves and one has none. You measure how far each water level drops.

items.p: Water moves up a plant only in the daytime.
items.why: False. At night the leaf holes are mostly closed and it is cool, so water moves up much more slowly. But it does not stop completely. Roots can even push a little water up at night, which is why you may find drops at the tips of grass blades at dawn.

items.p: In 1891, Eduard Strasburger killed all the living cells in long stems, and coloured water still climbed up them. Which idea did this show to be wrong?
opts: Water is pulled up by evaporation from the leaves
Living cells must pump water up the stem
items.why: If living pumps were needed, a dead stem could not lift water. But it did. So living pumps are not needed. Picking 'pulled by evaporation' misses that a dead stem can still let water evaporate from its top.

items.p: A suction pump can lift water about 10 metres. The tallest tree, Hyperion, is about 116 metres. About how many times taller is the tree than the suction limit?
items.why: 116 divided by 10 is 11.6, which is nearly 12. So the tree is about 12 times taller than the suction limit. Picking 100 times would need a tree about 1,000 metres tall.

items.p: In 2023, Lilach Hadany's team in Tel Aviv recorded thirsty tomato and tobacco plants making tiny clicks, too high for people to hear. Scientists disagree about what the clicks mean.

views.who: Lilach Hadany's team, as an idea to test
views.says: The clicks are real, and some moths and mice can hear sounds this high. Maybe animals or other plants listen and learn that a plant is thirsty.

views.who: Scientists who are not yet convinced
views.says: The clicks are most likely air bubbles forming as water threads snap in the tubes. Nobody has yet shown any animal or plant listening to them.

items.ask: Which view do you lean towards? Say what evidence would change your mind. Then say what the other side has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and names a test. For the listening idea: the clicks are real and loud enough for some animals. Against it: so far no one has seen an animal act on them. Evidence that would decide it: for example, moths choosing not to lay eggs on clicking plants. A strong answer agrees with both sides that the clicks come from the stretched water threads in the tubes.
items.why: This is a live question. What makes an answer strong is knowing the difference between what has been recorded and what is still only an idea to test.

items.p: Scientists all agree on exactly how much of the water rising from land into the air comes out of plants.
items.why: False. One study in 2013 said plants send up about 80 to 90 out of every 100 drops rising from land. Later studies said about 60. They agree it is a big share, but not on the exact amount.

items.p: A redwood's leaves at the very top are much smaller than their lower leaves. What might that tell scientists?
opts: Water barely reaches the top, so the top leaves stay small and thirsty
items.why: George Koch's team found the top leaves of the tallest redwoods were small and thirsty. It was as if water could barely be pulled that high. This helped them estimate how tall a tree can grow. Picking 'less light' is wrong, because the top gets the most light of all.

items.p: A plant's xylem tubes are very narrow, far thinner than a hair, and there are thousands of them. Why might many narrow tubes work better than one wide pipe?
items.a: If an air bubble gets into one tube, the water thread there snaps. With thousands of tubes, the others keep carrying water, so the plant does not dry out. In a narrow tube, water also clings to the walls and to itself, so the thread holds together better.
items.why: A strong answer sees that many tubes are back-ups for each other. One broken thread does not stop the whole plant.

items.p: Astronauts on the space station grow plants in small pillows with wicks. Why?
opts: In space, water does not drip down into the soil, so wicks bring it to the roots
Plants in space do not need water
The pillows keep the plants warm
To stop the plants floating off
items.why: On Earth, gravity pulls water down around the roots. In space, water floats in clumps. A wick moves water by capillary action, which works without gravity. Picking 'to stop floating off' is partly true for the plants, but the wicks are for the water.

items.p: Is this a PUSH from the roots or a PULL from the leaves?
items: sap dripping from a cut vine stump
Push from the roots
water climbing fastest on a hot sunny afternoon
Pull from the leaves
a drop at a grass tip at dawn
Push from the roots
the leafy stem drinking more than the bare stem
Pull from the leaves
items.a: see items
items.why: Dripping stumps and dawn drops at grass tips show the small push from the roots. Fast drinking in the sun and the leafy stem show the much bigger pull from the leaves.

items.p: A big forest is cut down. Months later, the farms downwind get less rain. Explain how cutting the trees could lead to less rain.
items.a: Trees pull water up from the soil and let most of it out through their leaves as vapour. That vapour rises, forms clouds and falls as rain further along. With the trees gone, much less water goes up into the air, so less rain falls downwind.
items.why: A strong answer follows the water from the soil, through the trees, into the air and back down as rain. Scientists have measured this link in places like the Amazon.
items.context: Leaves let out huge amounts of water vapour. A big tree can let out about 200 litres on a hot day.

items.p: The tiny electric pulls that hold water molecules together are called hydrogen ____.
items.why: Hydrogen bonds join the hydrogen end of one water molecule to the oxygen end of the next.

items.p: Why is the air under a big neem tree cooler than in a sunny car park, even apart from the shade?
opts: Water evaporating from the leaves takes heat away, like sweat drying on skin
Leaves blow cold air like a fan
items.why: Turning water into vapour takes heat energy. The leaves give it up, so they and the air around them cool down. Picking 'blow like a fan' is close, because moving leaves do stir the air, but the main cooling is evaporation.

items.p: In Be Stephen Hales, a plant lost 32 grams from Monday to Tuesday, a sunny day. The plant weighed 480 grams on Tuesday and 466 grams on Wednesday, a cloudy day. On which day did they lose more water, and why?
opts: The sunny day, because water evaporates faster in sun
The cloudy day, because clouds pull water
The cloudy day, because it was 14 grams
items.why: 480 take away 466 is 14 grams on the cloudy day, less than 32 grams on the sunny day. Sun makes leaves lose water faster. Picking 'the cloudy day, because it was 14 grams' means finding the right number but comparing it the wrong way.
items.context: In the Be Stephen Hales project, you cover a pot's soil so water can only leave through the leaves. Then you weigh the plant every day.

items.p: The water in your glass may once have been inside a dinosaur, a cloud and a tree. Explain how the same water could have been in all three.
items.a: Water goes round and round. A tree pulls water up and lets it out into the air. It becomes a cloud and falls as rain. A dinosaur drinks it and breathes it out. The same water keeps travelling for millions of years.
items.why: A good answer describes water moving between living things, the air and rain, again and again.

items.p: Bose was a great scientist, and he was wrong about how water climbs. What does this tell you about how science works?
items.a: Even great scientists can be wrong. Other scientists test their ideas. When the evidence shows an idea is wrong, science changes, even if the person was famous. Being wrong is part of finding out.
items.why: Any answer that says ideas are tested with evidence, and that anyone can be wrong, is right.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether wind makes a plant lose water faster. Say what you will change, what you will keep the same, and what you will measure.
items.a: I will use two similar leafy stems in two identical bottles with oil on top. One will be in front of a fan, the other in the same room with no fan. I will keep the light, the warmth and the stems the same. I will measure how far the water drops in each bottle after a day.
items.why: A good answer changes only the wind, keeps everything else the same, and measures the water used.

items.p: Draw a tall tree with a chain of water inside from the roots to the leaves. Mark where the pull starts, where the Sun's energy comes in, and what holds the chain together.
items.a: A tree with a line of water from the roots up the trunk to the leaves. An arrow shows vapour leaving a leaf hole at the top, labelled 'the pull starts here'. The Sun shines on the leaf, labelled 'energy'. The chain is labelled 'water molecules holding on to each other (cohesion)'.
items.why: This one drawing holds the whole idea: water leaving at the top pulls the chain up, the Sun pays for it, and cohesion stops the chain from snapping.

experiments.title: The Blue Climb: coloured water up a stem
experiments.question: Does water really travel up a stem to the leaves and petals? Where does it go, and how long does it take?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the colour go up the stem? Will it reach the petals? How long will it take? Draw your guess, and say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Stand one leaf or flower in coloured water and one in plain water. Use the same kind, cut the same way, in the same place. Only the colour of the water is different. Check both at the same times.
results_table: What the petals or leaf look like

materials.item: 2 pale inner leaves of a cabbage, each with its thick white rib, or 2 white carnations from a flower seller. White chrysanthemums (sevanthi) also work, but more slowly. If you grow balsam, 2 balsam stems work well too
2 clear glasses or jars
food colour, dark blue or red: about 1 teaspoon of liquid, or 2 big pinches of powder
a bowl of water and a kitchen knife, for a grown-up only
a clock and a pencil, and a ruler if you use a balsam stem
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Food colour stains clothes and hands, so put newspaper down.

schedule.what: Guess, set up the two glasses, and look after 2 hours and before bed.
Look the next day. A grown-up cuts the stem across. Look for coloured dots. Draw and finish.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at each check. Draw the petals or leaf, and the cut end of the stem.

flow.do: 1. Fill both glasses halfway with water. 2. Stir food colour into one glass until it is as dark as ink. Use about 1 teaspoon of liquid colour, or 2 big pinches of powder. 3. Ask your child to guess what will happen, and why, and to draw the guess.
flow.say: This glass has coloured water and this one has plain water. We'll stand a pale leaf or a white flower in each. What will happen to the one in the coloured water? Why do you think so? Draw your guess.
flow.kid: Put water in two glasses. Add lots of colour to one. What will happen to a pale leaf or white flower in it? Why? Draw your guess.

ask.q: Where do you think the colour will go?
good: Up the stem.
Into the petals.
It will stay in the glass.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. A child who says 'it will stay in the glass' has a clear idea that we can test. Do not correct it yet. Use plenty of colour, because pale water gives a result too faint to see.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Blue Climb. You stand pale leaves or white flowers in coloured water and plain water, and watch where the colour goes.

flow.do: 1. Hold the bottom of each stem under water in a bowl. Cut about 1 to 2 cm off it at a slant, under the water. 2. Stand one stem in each glass straight away. 3. Write down the time. 4. Put both glasses in a bright, airy place out of direct sun, such as near an open window or a fan.
flow.say: I'm cutting the stems under water, so no air gets into the tubes inside. Air bubbles would block them. Now let's write down the time.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the stems under water. Stand one in each glass. Write down the time.
flow.parent: Cutting under water is what flower sellers do. A stem cut in the air can take in a little air, which blocks some tubes. Moving air helps the petals lose water, and that pulls the coloured water up faster.

flow.do: 1. After 2 hours, look closely at the petals and the stem. 2. If you used a see-through balsam stem, measure how high the colour has climbed with the ruler. 3. Write what you see in the table. 4. Look again before bed.
flow.say: Let's look. Can you see colour anywhere yet? Where is it?
flow.kid: After two hours, look closely. Can you see colour? Where is it? Write it down.

good: No, it is still white.
No. So the colour came from the water.

flow.parent: Colour usually shows first as thin lines in the veins and at the petal edges. In a carnation this can take a few hours. In a cabbage leaf, look at the veins near its top edge. It may take most of a day. In a see-through balsam stem you can watch a coloured line rise. If you see nothing at bedtime, that is normal.

flow.do: The next day, look at the petals or the leaf with the magnifying glass. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Look at it now. Where is the colour darkest? What do the lines look like?
flow.kid: Look at the petals or the leaf. Where is the colour darkest? Draw the lines you see.

check.q: In the Blue Climb, the pale leaf or white petals now have coloured lines. What does that show?
options: The flower changed colour by itself overnight
Water climbed up the stem and spread through tiny tubes into the petals
The colour soaked in through the outside of the petals or leaf
check.why: The only way the colour could get up there is with the water, up through the stem. The plain-water one stayed pale, so it did not change by itself. The top of the leaf and the petals never touched the coloured water, so it did not soak in from outside. Picking 'by itself' usually means the plain-water one was not compared. That is why we set up two glasses.

flow.wait: Leave them for a day: at least 12 hours, and up to 24.
flow.parent: If there is still no colour after a day, cut 2 cm off each stem under water again and add more colour. Move the glass near a fan or an open window, and look again that evening. Fresh leaves and flowers work best, because old, tired ones drink slowly. Rajnigandha stalks often take up colour too slowly to see at home.

flow.do: 1. Cut across the coloured stem about halfway up. For a cabbage leaf, cut across its thick white middle rib. 2. Let your child look at the cut end with the magnifying glass.
flow.say: Look at the cut end. What do you see? Why do you think the colour is in dots, and not everywhere?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the stem across. Look at the end. Can you see coloured dots? Why dots?

ask.q: Why are there dots, and not colour everywhere?
good: The water only went up the tubes.
The tubes are in bundles, not everywhere.

flow.parent: In a flower stem the dots sit in a ring. In a cabbage rib they sit in a row. They are bundles of xylem, the water tubes, and the coloured water climbed only through them. A flower stem is thin, so use the magnifying glass. A cabbage rib shows the dots most clearly.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Work out how long the colour took to reach the petals.
flow.say: We started at this time. We first saw colour in the petals or the leaf at this time. How many hours did the water take to climb up?
flow.kid: Look at your table. When did you first see colour? How many hours was that?
flow.think: A neem tree has no glass of coloured water. Their water tubes are hidden in their wood. How could you find out how fast water climbs in a tree?

chart.title: Made-up example: how high the colour climbed up a see-through balsam stem
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: water climbs up a stem through tiny tubes and goes into the petals. What I saw: the next day the petals had blue lines and blue edges, and the cut stem had a ring of blue dots. The plain flower stayed white. Why: the water carried the colour with it up the tubes, to the petals, where the water leaves into the air.

experiments.context: This is the coloured-water experiment. You stand a pale leaf or a white flower in coloured water. The colour shows the hidden path that water takes up a plant.

experiments.title: Leafy or Bare? Which stem drinks more?
experiments.question: Do the leaves help to pull water up a stem? Does a leafy stem drink more than a bare one?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a stem with leaves drink more, less, or the same as a stem with its leaves taken off? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two stems from the same plant, the same length. Put them in two bottles that are exactly the same, with the same amount of water, in the same place. Pour a thin layer of oil on the water in both. Then no water can evaporate from the bottle itself. Only one thing is different: one stem keeps its leaves.

materials.item: 2 leafy stems about the same size, such as 2 pudina (mint) stems from the vegetable bunch, or 2 stems from a potted hibiscus or coleus
2 identical small clear plastic water bottles, filled with water up into their narrow necks, or 2 clear test tubes
a spoon of cooking oil
a marker pen and a ruler with millimetres

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the stems. Wipe up any oil spills, as they make the floor slippery.

schedule.what: Guess. Cut two stems, pull the leaves off one, set up the bottles with oil, and mark the water levels.
Mark and measure the new water levels.
Measure again, draw a bar chart, and finish.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each stem, as tall as its total drop in millimetres.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which stem will drink more, and to write the guess down.
flow.say: We'll put two stems in water. One keeps its leaves. One has its leaves taken off. Which one will drink more water? Why?
flow.kid: Two stems in water. One has leaves. One has none. Which will drink more? Write your guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Leafy or Bare?. You test whether a stem with leaves pulls up more water than a stem with no leaves.

flow.do: 1. Cut two similar stems, each about 20 cm long, under water. 2. Pinch all the leaves off one stem. 3. Fill both bottles with the same amount of water, up into the narrow neck. 4. Put one stem in each. 5. Pour a thin layer of oil on the water in each bottle. 6. Mark the water level on each bottle with the marker.
flow.say: The oil is a lid. It stops water drying straight out of the bottle. So any water that goes must go through the stem.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut two stems. Pinch the leaves off one. Put each in a bottle. Add a little oil on top. Mark the water level.

check.q: In the Leafy or Bare test, why do we pour oil on top of the water?
options: To feed the stems
So water can't evaporate from the bottle itself, only through the stem
To make the water heavier
check.why: Water can evaporate from any open surface, even with no plant. A thin oil layer stops that. Then if the water level drops, the water must have gone up the stem. Picking 'to feed the stems' usually means thinking plants eat whatever is put in their water. The oil is only a lid.

flow.parent: Keep the water level in the narrow neck of the bottle. In a wide part, the same amount of water makes only a tiny drop in the level.

flow.do: 1. The next day, mark the new water level on each bottle. 2. Measure the drop from the first mark, in millimetres. 3. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Let's measure. How many millimetres has the water gone down in each bottle?
flow.kid: Mark the new water level. Measure how far it dropped, in millimetres. Write it in the table.
flow.parent: Read the ruler at eye level. Millimetres are the tiny marks between the centimetre numbers. Ten millimetres make one centimetre.

flow.do: 1. On day 3, measure again. 2. Add up the total drop for each stem. 3. Draw a bar chart, one bar for each stem.
flow.say: Let's draw one bar for each stem. Which bar is taller? What does that tell us?
flow.kid: Measure again. Draw one bar for each stem. Which bar is taller?

check.q: In the Leafy or Bare test, the leafy stem's water dropped 18 mm. The bare stem's dropped 3 mm. What does this show?
options: Leaves help pull water up the stem
Bare stems are thirstier
The bottles were different
check.why: Everything was the same except the leaves. The leafy stem used much more water. So the leaves must be what pulls the water up, by letting it escape into the air. Picking 'the bottles were different' is a good worry. That is why we used two bottles that are exactly the same.

flow.do: Talk about why the bare stem still drank a little.
flow.say: The bare stem still drank a tiny bit. Where could that water have gone?
flow.kid: The bare stem drank a tiny bit too. Where did that water go?
flow.parent: A little water evaporates from the stem's skin and the cut top, and a little soaks into the stem. Some stems also have a few leaf holes in the stem's skin.
flow.think: If you pulled most of the leaves off a plant, would they need less water? Why do gardeners sometimes cut back plants when they move them?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the leaves pull water up the stem. What I saw: in 2 days the leafy stem's water went down 18 mm. The bare stem's went down only 3 mm. Why: water escapes from the leaves into the air, and that pulls more water up behind it. The bare stem has no leaves to let the water out.

experiments.title: The Sweating Branch: sun or shade?
experiments.question: Does a leafy branch give off more water in the sun or in the shade?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will tie a clear bag over a branch in the sun, and another over a branch in the shade. Which bag will collect more water? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two potted plants of the same kind and about the same size, or two similar branches of one plant. Use two bags that are the same. Tie them on at the same time and leave them for the same time. Only one thing is different: sun or shade.
results_table: What the inside of the bag looks like
Water collected (spoons, or millilitres with a syringe)

materials.item: 2 clear plastic bags of the same size, without holes
2 pieces of thread or rubber bands
2 similar potted plants, one in the sun and one in the shade, or one plant with two similar leafy branches
a teaspoon, or a medicine syringe without a needle, to measure the water

experiments.safety: Plastic bags are never for heads or faces. Keep them away from very young children. Take the bags off the plants afterwards, so the leaves do not overheat.

schedule.what: Tie the bags on, wait 2 hours, then look, measure and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw both bags, showing the mist and drops inside each one.

flow.do: 1. Put one potted plant in bright sun, on a balcony or a sunny windowsill, and the other in the shade indoors. 2. If you have only one plant, use two branches, and shade one with a cone of newspaper. 3. Ask your child to guess which bag will get more water, and why.
flow.say: We're going to catch the water that leaves the leaves. Which bag do you think will get more, the one in the sun or the one in the shade? Why?
flow.kid: One plant in the sun. One in the shade. Which will give off more water? Why? Guess!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sweating Branch. You tie clear bags over two leafy branches and catch the water that the leaves let out.

flow.do: 1. Slip a bag over each branch without picking it. 2. Tie the open end loosely but firmly round the branch's stem. 3. Write down the time.
flow.say: Slide the bag over the leaves. Tie it round the stem, not too tight, so we don't hurt the plant.
flow.kid: Slide a bag over each branch. Ask a grown-up to tie it round the stem. Write down the time.

flow.do: 1. After 2 hours, look at both bags without taking them off. 2. Gently tap the drops down into a corner of each bag.
flow.say: Look inside the bags. What do you see? Where did those drops come from?
flow.kid: After two hours, look at the bags. Misty? Drops? Tap the drops into a corner.

ask.q: Where did the water in the bag come from?
good: From the leaves.
It came up the stem and out of the leaves.
Water vapour from the leaves turned back into drops.

flow.parent: Expect mist within half an hour in the sun. A small branch may give only a few drops, and a big leafy one a teaspoon or more. Both are real results.

flow.do: 1. Take each bag off carefully and pour the water into a spoon or suck it up with the syringe. 2. Write how much each bag collected.
flow.say: Let's measure. How much water came out of each branch in just two hours?
flow.kid: Take the bags off gently. Pour the water into a spoon. Which bag has more?

check.q: In the Sweating Branch test, which bag usually collects more water?
options: The bag on the branch in the sun
The bag on the branch in the shade
Both always get exactly the same
check.why: Sun warms the leaves, makes them open their holes, and makes water evaporate faster. So the sunny branch lets out more water vapour, which turns back into drops on the inside of the bag. Picking 'the shade' usually means thinking a cool place is wetter, so it would collect more. But the drops come from the plant, not the air.

flow.do: Talk about what this means for a whole tree.
flow.say: This was one small branch, for two hours. A big tree has thousands of branches, all day. How much water do you think a big tree lets out on a hot day?
flow.kid: This was one small branch. A big tree has thousands. How much water does a whole tree let out?
flow.parent: A big tree on a hot day can send up hundreds of litres of water. That is many buckets, lifted by the Sun and let into the air.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: leaves let out more water in the sun. What I saw: the sunny bag had about a teaspoon of water. The shady bag had only a few drops. Why: the sun warms the leaves and makes the water evaporate faster, so more water leaves through the leaf holes.

experiments.context: In this experiment you tie clear bags over two leafy branches, one in the sun and one in the shade. You catch and measure the water the leaves let out.

activities.title: The Two-Colour Flower

materials.item: 1 white carnation with a long stem, from a flower seller, or a pale inner cabbage leaf with a long white rib
2 small glasses, and 2 food colours, such as blue and red
a sharp knife, kitchen scissors and sticky tape, for a grown-up

activities.safety: Only a grown-up uses the knife. Split the stem slowly, on a chopping board.

schedule.what: Split the stem, stand each half in a different colour, and guess.
Look at the flower the next day, and draw it.

activities.record: Draw the flower before and after. Colour in where each colour went.

flow.do: 1. On a chopping board, split the bottom of the stem lengthways into two halves. Start at the cut end and stop about 8 cm up. 2. Wrap a bit of sticky tape round the stem just above the split, so it does not split further.
flow.say: I'm splitting the stem into two legs. One leg will stand in blue water, and the other in red.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to split the stem into two legs. Put tape above the split so it stops there.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two-Colour Flower. You split a white flower's stem into two halves and stand each half in a different colour.

flow.do: 1. Put the two glasses side by side, one blue and one red. 2. Stand one leg of the stem in each glass. 3. Under the water, snip a little off the end of each leg with the scissors, so no air gets into the tubes. 4. Ask your child to guess what the flower will look like tomorrow.
flow.say: One leg drinks blue and one drinks red. What will the flower look like tomorrow? Will it go purple? Half and half? Draw your guess.
flow.kid: Stand one leg in blue water and one in red water. Ask a grown-up to snip each end under the water. What will the flower look like tomorrow? Draw it.

flow.do: The next day, look at the flower closely and compare it with the guess.
flow.say: Look! Which side is blue, and which side is red? Did the colours mix?
flow.kid: Look at your flower. Is it purple? Or is one side blue and one side red?

check.q: A white flower's stem was split, and each half stood in a different colour. The flower came out half blue and half red. What does that show?
options: The tubes from each half of the stem go to their own part of the flower
The colours fought and the strongest won
All the water mixes together in the middle of the stem
check.why: Each water tube runs on its own, from the bottom of the stem to one part of the flower. Water in one tube does not mix with water in the tubes beside it. So the blue tubes fed one side and the red tubes fed the other. Picking 'all the water mixes' is a very sensible guess, because the stem looks like one solid thing. The flower shows it is really a bundle of separate tubes.

flow.think: If one root of a big tree is cut, which branches might go thirsty?

activities.context: In this activity you split a white flower's stem into two halves. Each half drinks a different colour. The flower shows which tubes go where.

activities.title: The Water Chain (act it out)

materials.item: a staircase, or a line of cushions on the floor as steps
3 or more people, or soft toys for a child playing alone

activities.safety: Walk slowly on the stairs and hold the railing. Do not pull hard on anyone's arms.

schedule.what: Act out water being pulled up a tube, and a bubble breaking the chain.

activities.record: Draw the chain of water people on the stairs, with the top one floating off as vapour.

flow.do: Everyone stands in a line up the stairs, holding hands. The bottom person is at the root. The top person is at the leaf hole.
flow.say: We are water molecules inside one tiny tube in a stem. We hold hands, because water sticks to itself. The bottom of the stairs is the root. The top is a leaf.
flow.kid: Stand in a line up the stairs. Hold hands. You are water inside a stem. The top of the stairs is the leaf.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Chain. People hold hands up a staircase to act out how water is pulled up a plant.

flow.do: 1. The top person lets go and walks away, waving: they have evaporated into the air. 2. Everyone steps up one stair. 3. A new person, or a toy, joins at the bottom. 4. Repeat a few times.
flow.say: The sun warms the leaf. The top molecule evaporates and floats away. Everyone steps up. A new molecule comes in at the root. That's how water climbs!
flow.kid: The top person waves and floats away. Everyone steps up one stair. Someone new joins at the bottom. Again!

good: The one who left at the top.
The sun, by making the top one evaporate.

flow.parent: This is the cohesion-tension idea. Evaporation at the leaf pulls on the whole chain. The chain holds because water molecules cling to each other.

flow.do: Now one person in the middle lets go of hands: they are an air bubble. The top person leaves again. Can the people below the gap step up?
flow.say: Oh no, an air bubble! Someone in the middle let go. Now when the top drop leaves, can the bottom of the chain still be pulled up?
flow.kid: An air bubble! Someone in the middle lets go. Now the top one leaves. Can the bottom of the chain still move up?

check.q: In the Water Chain, someone in the middle let go of hands, like an air bubble. What happens to the people below the gap?
options: They keep stepping up as before
They get stuck, because nothing is pulling them any more
They jump over the gap
check.why: The pull only travels along hands that are held. Below the gap, nothing is pulling. In a real plant, an air bubble in a tube breaks the thread of water. Then that tube stops carrying water. Picking 'keep stepping up' usually means thinking the roots push the water. Roots push only a little.

flow.do: Talk about how a plant copes with bubbles.
flow.say: A plant has thousands of tubes side by side. If one gets a bubble, the water can go round it through the others.
flow.kid: A plant has thousands of tubes. If one gets a bubble, water uses the others.
flow.think: Why do flower sellers cut stems under water? Think about the air bubble person.

activities.context: This is a short play on a staircase. People hold hands to act out water climbing up a tube in a plant, pulled from the top.

activities.title: Bring Back the Wilted Coriander

materials.item: a bunch of coriander, palak or mint that has gone floppy
a glass of cool water and a bowl of water
kitchen scissors, used by a grown-up

schedule.what: Revive a wilted bunch, and check after an hour.

activities.record: Draw the bunch before and after. Write how long they took to stand up.

flow.do: Leave a small bunch of coriander out of the fridge for a few hours until the leaves wilt. Feel them with your child.
flow.say: Feel these leaves. They are soft and floppy. Why do you think they have gone like this?
flow.kid: Touch the floppy coriander. Are they soft or crisp? Why do you think they drooped?

good: It lost water.
They are out of the soil, so they cannot drink.
The water left through the leaves.

flow.context: This is the first step of Bring Back the Wilted Coriander. You take a floppy bunch of coriander and help them drink until they stand up again.

flow.do: 1. Hold the stems under water in the bowl. 2. Snip about 1 cm off the bottoms, under the water. 3. Stand the bunch in the glass of cool water straight away.
flow.say: We cut under water, so no air bubbles get into the tubes. Now the leaves can pull water up again.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to snip the stems under water. Stand the bunch in a glass of water.

flow.do: After an hour, feel and look at the bunch again. Compare with the drawing.
flow.say: Feel them now. What changed? Where did the stiffness come from?
flow.kid: After one hour, touch them again. Are they crisp now? How did the water get into the leaves?

check.q: The wilted coriander stood in water for an hour and became crisp again. Why?
options: Water went up the stems and filled the cells, so they pushed against each other and stood firm
The cold water froze the leaves stiff
The leaves soaked water in from the air
check.why: Each cell has a stretchy bag inside. When water fills the bags, the cells press hard on each other, like water balloons packed in a bag. That makes leaves and stems firm. Picking 'froze stiff' mixes up cool water with ice. Picking 'from the air' misses that the water came up from the glass, through the stems.

flow.do: Talk about how flower and vegetable sellers keep things fresh.
flow.say: Next time we go to the vegetable market, look at how sellers keep greens fresh. Do they sprinkle water? Keep them in the shade? Stand them in buckets?
flow.kid: At the market, look at how sellers keep greens fresh. Water? Shade? Buckets?
flow.think: A plant in soil can wilt at noon and stand up again in the evening. What changes between noon and evening?

activities.context: In this activity you take a bunch of coriander that has gone floppy and help them drink. It shows why plants wilt, and how water makes them firm.

activities.title: Bubbles from a Leaf: find the hidden holes

materials.item: 2 or 3 freshly picked leaves, such as hibiscus, money plant or rose
a glass bowl and hot water from a kettle that has cooled for 5 minutes, not boiling
a magnifying glass
optional: a cheap pocket microscope, clear nail polish and clear sticky tape

activities.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water. Let boiled water cool for 5 minutes first, and keep small hands out of it. Nail polish is used only by a grown-up, in an airy room.

schedule.what: Watch bubbles come out of a leaf, and look for leaf holes.

activities.record: Draw the leaf, with dots where the bubbles came out. Write which side had more bubbles.

flow.do: 1. Fill the glass bowl with hot water from a kettle that has cooled for 5 minutes. 2. Push a fresh leaf under the water with a spoon and hold it there. 3. Watch both sides of the leaf closely for a minute or two.
flow.say: Watch the leaf carefully. Do you see tiny bubbles? Which side are they coming from?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up for hot water in a bowl. They push a leaf under. Watch closely. See tiny bubbles?

ask.q: Where are the bubbles coming from?
good: The underside of the leaf.
Tiny holes in the leaf.

flow.context: This is the first step of Bubbles from a Leaf. You hold a fresh leaf under hot water and watch air bubble out of its tiny holes.
flow.parent: Tiny silver bubbles should appear within a minute, mostly on the underside. If you see very few, try a thicker leaf, or hotter water.

flow.do: 1. Turn the leaf over and compare the two sides. 2. Count the bubbles on each side for one minute.
flow.say: Turn the leaf over. Which side has more bubbles? Where do you think this air was hiding?
flow.kid: Count the bubbles on each side for one minute. Which side has more?

check.q: A leaf held under hot water gives off tiny bubbles, mostly from its underside. Why?
options: The leaf is breathing out like a fish
Air inside the leaf swells in the hot water and escapes through tiny holes, which are mostly on the underside
The leaf is melting
check.why: A leaf is full of tiny air spaces, joined to the outside by thousands of holes called stomata. Heat makes the air swell and squeeze out of the holes. Many leaves have most of their holes underneath, out of the hot sun, which helps them lose less water. Picking 'breathing like a fish' is a lovely idea. But these bubbles come from the hot water making the air swell.

flow.do: Optional, with a pocket microscope. 1. A grown-up paints a small patch of clear nail polish on the underside of a leaf. 2. Let it dry for 10 minutes. 3. Press clear sticky tape on it and peel it off. Stick the tape on a glass slide or a clear plastic sheet. 4. Look at it under the microscope.
flow.say: This peel is a copy of the leaf's skin. Can you see little shapes like mouths, or coffee beans? Those are the leaf holes, with their two guard cells.
flow.kid: Look through the microscope. See tiny shapes like mouths? Those are the leaf's holes!
flow.parent: A cheap 60 to 120 times pocket microscope is enough. If you have no microscope, skip this step. A phone camera through a magnifying glass sometimes works too.

activities.context: In this activity you put a fresh leaf in hot water and watch tiny bubbles come out. They show where a leaf's hidden holes are.

activities.title: Climbing Tea and the Great Straw Test

materials.item: a strip of paper towel or tissue, and a cup of tea or coloured water
6 drinking straws (paper ones work if the joins are taped well), sticky tape, and a glass of water
a ruler

activities.safety: Use cool tea or coloured water, never hot. Do not share straws.

schedule.what: Watch water creep up paper, then test how high you can suck water with joined straws.

activities.record: Write how high the tea climbed up the paper after 10 minutes. Write how many joined straws you could still drink through.

flow.do: 1. Hang a strip of paper towel so its bottom end just dips into a cup of coloured water. 2. Watch for 10 minutes. 3. Measure how high the colour climbs.
flow.say: Watch the water climb up the paper all by itself. It clings to the paper and to itself. That's called capillary action.
flow.kid: Dip the end of a paper strip into coloured water. Watch it climb! Measure how high it goes in 10 minutes.

ask.q: Did it keep climbing for ever?
good: No, it slowed down and stopped.
It only went a few centimetres.

flow.context: This is the first step of Climbing Tea and the Great Straw Test. You watch water creep up paper by itself, and test how high you can suck water through straws.

flow.do: 1. Put the glass of water on the floor. 2. Drink a little through one straw, held straight up. 3. Tape two straws end to end, and try again. 4. Keep adding straws, and taping the joins tightly, until it gets very hard.
flow.say: Sucking takes air out of the straw. Then the air outside pushes the water up. Let's see how long a straw you can still drink from.
flow.kid: Drink through one straw. Now tape two straws together and try. Then three. When does it get too hard?
flow.parent: Tape every join well, because leaks of air make it fail early. Many children manage 3 to 5 straws. Even a perfect pump could only lift water about 10 metres this way.

flow.do: Compare the paper, the straw and a tall tree.
flow.say: The paper lifted water a few centimetres. The best pump in the world could lift it about 10 metres by sucking. But the tallest tree is about 116 metres tall. So how does a tree do it?
flow.kid: Paper lifts water a little. Sucking lifts it up to 10 metres at most. The tallest tree is 116 metres! How?

check.q: Paper lifts water a few centimetres, and sucking can lift it about 10 metres at most. How does water reach the top of a 116 metre tree?
options: The tree sucks very hard, like a giant straw
The leaves let water evaporate, and that pulls up unbroken threads of water that hold together
The water creeps up like tea up a tissue
check.why: A tree is not a straw. A straw needs air to push the water up, and that can only work up to about 10 metres. Creeping up thin gaps only lifts water a little way. Instead, each tube holds a thread of water that hangs together, and evaporation pulls it up from the top. Picking 'a giant straw' is a natural guess. This test shows why it cannot be the answer.

activities.context: In this activity you watch coloured water creep up a paper strip. Then you test how high you can suck water through joined straws. Both are compared with how a tall tree lifts water.

activities.title: The Dawn Drop Hunt (if you have a garden or a park nearby)

materials.item: a magnifying glass
a patch of grass, a lawn or a park, early in the morning

activities.safety: Go outside only with a grown-up. Wear chappals on wet grass.

schedule.what: Look for water drops on grass and leaves just after sunrise.

activities.record: Draw a grass blade with a drop at its tip. Draw a leaf covered in tiny dew drops. Write how they are different.

flow.do: Just after sunrise, go to a patch of grass. Look closely at the tips of the grass blades, and at leaves of other small plants.
flow.say: Look at the very tips of the grass blades. Some have one round drop sitting right at the tip. Other leaves are covered all over with tiny drops.
flow.kid: Go out early with a grown-up. Look at grass tips. Is there one drop right at the end? Or tiny drops all over?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dawn Drop Hunt. Early in the morning, you look for two kinds of water drops on grass and leaves.
flow.parent: Drops at grass tips appear on cool, damp mornings, often after a warm day when the soil is wet. If you see none, try again another morning. A potted colocasia or tomato plant on a balcony sometimes shows them too.

flow.do: Explain the two kinds of drops.
flow.say: Tiny drops all over a leaf are usually dew. Water vapour in the cool night air turned back into drops on the cold leaf. But one big drop right at the tip came from inside the plant. The roots pushed water up in the night, and it was squeezed out of special holes at the tip.
flow.kid: Tiny drops all over are dew, from the air. One drop at the tip came from inside the plant! The roots pushed it out.

check.q: On the Dawn Drop Hunt, you find one round drop sitting right at the tip of a grass blade. Where did it most likely come from?
options: From inside the plant, pushed up by the roots in the night
From a cloud
From an insect
check.why: At night the leaf holes are mostly closed, so little water leaves as vapour. But roots can keep pushing water up a little. The water is squeezed out of tiny openings at the leaf tip. Scientists call this guttation. Dew is different: it forms from the air, as tiny drops all over a surface. Picking 'from a cloud' mixes it up with rain.

flow.do: Come back after an hour of sun and look again.
flow.say: Where have the drops gone? Into the air? Back into the leaf?
flow.kid: Come back in an hour. Where did the drops go?
flow.think: At night the roots push. In the day the leaves pull. Which do you think is stronger?

activities.context: This is an early-morning hunt for water drops on grass. You learn to tell two kinds of drops apart. Dew comes from the air. Other drops are pushed out of the leaf tips by the plant.

projects.title: Be Stephen Hales: weigh a plant's thirst

materials.item: a small potted plant, such as tulsi, coleus or a chilli plant
a kitchen weighing scale that shows grams
a plastic bag or cling film, and a rubber band
a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: Lift the pot carefully with both hands. Cover only the soil and pot, never the leaves.

schedule.what: Water the plant, seal the pot and soil in plastic, and weigh it.
Weigh it at the same time. Write the weather.
Weigh it at the same time. Write the weather.
Weigh it at the same time. Write the weather.
Weigh it, work out how much water the plant lost each day, draw a bar chart, then water the plant and uncover the pot.

projects.record: A table of the weight each day, the weather each day, and the grams lost since the day before. Then a bar chart of grams lost each day.

flow.do: 1. Water the plant well and let the pot drain for an hour. 2. Wrap the pot and the soil in a plastic bag. Tie it round the base of the stem, so only the leaves are open to the air. 3. Weigh the whole thing and write it down.
flow.say: About 300 years ago, Stephen Hales did this with a sunflower. We've covered the soil, so water can only escape through the leaves. If the plant gets lighter, the lost weight is water that went out of the leaves.
flow.kid: Water the plant. Wrap the pot and soil in plastic. Leave the leaves open. Weigh it. Write the number.
flow.context: This is the first step of Be Stephen Hales. You weigh a potted plant every day to find out how much water they let out through their leaves.
flow.parent: If you don't have a kitchen scale, borrow one, or do the Leafy or Bare test instead. It measures the water a plant uses with a ruler.

flow.do: 1. Each day, at the same time, weigh the plant. 2. Write the weight and the weather: sunny, cloudy, rainy or windy.
flow.say: Same time every day, so it's fair. How many grams lighter is it today? Was it a sunny day?
flow.kid: Weigh the plant at the same time each day. Write the number and the weather.
flow.parent: One gram of weight lost is about one millilitre of water, a fifth of a teaspoon. A small plant may lose 10 to 50 grams a day, more on hot dry days.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, weigh it once more. 2. Work out the grams lost each day by taking each day's weight away from the day before. 3. Draw a bar for each day.
flow.say: Yesterday it weighed this much, today this much. Take one from the other to find what the plant lost. Which day did the plant lose the most? What was the weather?
flow.kid: Take today's weight away from yesterday's. That is the water the plant let out. Draw a bar for each day.

check.q: In the Be Stephen Hales project, the plant weighed 512 grams on Monday and 480 grams on Tuesday. How much water did the plant let out?
options: 32 grams
992 grams
480 grams
check.why: The weight lost is the difference. 512 take away 480 is 32. So the plant let out about 32 grams of water, which is about 32 millilitres. Picking 992 means adding the two weights instead of finding the difference.

chart.title: Made-up example: water a tulsi plant let out each day
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: 1. Look at the bar chart and the weather together. 2. Then water the plant and take the plastic off.
flow.say: Which weather made the plant let out the most water? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Look at your bars. Which day was tallest? What was the weather that day?

ask.q: Why did the plant lose more on sunny or windy days?
good: Water evaporates faster in sun and wind.
The leaves open their holes more in the sun.

flow.think: If this small plant lets out this much, how much does a big neem tree let out?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: plants let out more water on sunny, windy days. What I saw: my tulsi lost 38 grams on the windy day and only 8 grams on the rainy day. Why: wind and sun make water evaporate from the leaves faster, and damp air slows it down.

challenges.title: How High Can You Lift Water?
challenges.problem: Make water climb as high as you can above the water in a glass, without pouring, pumping or sucking. Plants lift water without any of those. How close can you get?
constraints: You cannot pick up the glass or pour from it.
No sucking, squeezing, spoons or syringes.
Use only things from home, like paper, cloth, string, sponge and chalk.
You have 24 hours. Measure the height of the wet line above the water in the glass.
materials: paper towel, tissue, cotton cloth, thick cotton string, a sponge, a stick of chalk
sticky tape, a ruler, and a pencil
a leafy stem and a small clear plastic bag, for the last idea
general: A strip of paper towel taped upright, with its bottom end in the water. The colour creeps up by capillary action, usually 10 centimetres or more.
A strip of cotton cloth or a thick cotton string, which works like the wick in a lamp.
A stick of chalk standing in the water. Chalk is full of tiny gaps, so the colour climbs inside it.
creative: Try narrower and wider strips of the same paper, to see whether the width changes the height.
Leave the best wick for a whole day. Watch how fast it climbs at first, and how it slows down and stops.
Stand a leafy stem in the water and tie a clear bag over its leaves. The water climbs the whole stem and comes out into the bag. A plant lifts water higher than any wick.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own water lifter. Draw it, try it, and measure how high the water climbed in 24 hours.

flow.do: 1. Fill a glass with coloured water. 2. Put the ruler, tape and the wick materials next to it.
flow.say: Here's the challenge. Make this water climb as high as you can, with no pouring and no sucking. A plant does it every day.
flow.kid: Fill a glass with coloured water. Make the water climb as high as you can. No pouring!
flow.parent: Wicks work by capillary action. Paper towel usually lifts water 10 to 15 centimetres in a few hours, and then stops. A leafy stem lifts it to the top of the stem and beyond, into the air.
flow.context: This is the first step of How High Can You Lift Water? You try to make coloured water climb as high as you can, without pouring or sucking.

flow.do: Before trying, draw or write three ideas together.
flow.say: Engineers plan first. What have you seen that makes water climb by itself? Which do you think will lift it highest, and why?
flow.kid: Plan first, like an engineer. Draw three ideas. What makes water climb by itself?

flow.do: 1. Try each idea. 2. Mark the wet line with a pencil after 10 minutes and after 1 hour. 3. Leave the best ones overnight. 4. In the morning, measure the height of the wet line above the water.
flow.say: Let's try your ideas. Which one is climbing highest? Let's mark the lines and leave them overnight.
flow.kid: Try each idea. Mark the wet line. Leave it overnight. Measure in the morning.

check.q: In How High Can You Lift Water?, a strip of paper towel lifts coloured water a few centimetres. What is lifting the water?
options: Magic in the paper
Capillary action: water clinging to the paper fibres and to itself
Gravity pulling it up
check.why: Water sticks to the paper's tiny fibres and to itself, so it creeps up the thin gaps. This is capillary action. Gravity pulls water down, so the climb slows and stops at a certain height. Plants use capillary action a little, but mostly they pull water up by evaporation.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas. Then invent your own.
flow.say: Here is what most people try, and some creative ideas. Can you beat them?
flow.kid: Read the usual ideas and the creative ones. Now invent your own. Can you beat them?
flow.think: Clay pots and cotton wicks have been used to water plants slowly for hundreds of years. Why might farmers want water to move slowly?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You try to make coloured water climb as high as you can, using only the tricks that wicks and plants use.

challenges.title: The Holiday Plant Sitter
challenges.problem: Your family is going away for a week. Design a way to keep a potted plant watered, with nobody at home.
constraints: It must not flood the plant, because roots need air too.
It must cost almost nothing, using things from home.
materials: thick cotton string or a strip of old cotton cloth
a small unglazed clay pot or diya
a clear plastic bag or a large clear bottle
general: A wick: one end of a cotton string in a bottle of water, the other end pushed into the soil. Water creeps along it into the soil.
An upside-down bottle with small holes in its cap, pushed into the soil, letting water out slowly.
A clear bag or cut bottle over the whole plant like a tent, so the water they let out stays inside and drips back.
creative: A small unglazed clay pot buried in the soil and filled with water. Water seeps out through the clay. Farmers in many dry places, including parts of India, have watered plants like this for a very long time.
Move the plant into the shade and out of the wind while you are away, so they let out less water.
Group several pots close together so they keep the air around them damp.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own plant sitter. Draw it, and test it for 3 days before the holiday. Each day, weigh the pot or push a finger into the soil to check it is still damp.

flow.do: Look at the plant together and talk about how they lose water.
flow.say: This plant lets water out of their leaves every day, and drinks from the soil. If nobody waters them for a week, what happens?
flow.kid: This plant loses water from their leaves every day. What happens if nobody waters them for a week?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Holiday Plant Sitter. You design a way to keep a potted plant watered for a week with nobody home.

flow.do: Draw three designs. For each one, ask: does it bring water in, or stop water leaving?
flow.say: There are two ways to help. Bring water in slowly. Or stop so much leaving. Which do your designs do?
flow.kid: Draw three designs. Does each one bring water in? Or stop water leaving?

check.q: In the Holiday Plant Sitter, you put a clear bag over the whole plant like a tent. How does that help?
options: It keeps the plant warm
The air inside gets damp, so less water leaves the leaves, and what does leave drips back down
It stops the plant from making food
check.why: Leaves lose water fastest into dry, moving air. Inside a bag, the air fills with water vapour and stays still. So the leaves lose much less, and the drops that form run back into the soil. Picking 'keeps the plant warm' is partly true, which is why the plant must stay out of hot sun while covered.

flow.do: 1. Build your best design. 2. Weigh the pot. 3. Test it for 3 days, weighing the pot each day.
flow.say: If the pot stays about the same weight, water is coming in as fast as it goes out. If it gets much lighter, the plant is drying.
flow.kid: Build your best design. Weigh the pot each day for 3 days. Is it staying heavy?
flow.parent: Keep the plant out of direct sun if they are under a bag, or they may overheat. Make sure the pot has a drainage hole so a leaky bottle cannot drown the roots.

flow.do: Compare your design with the usual and creative ideas, and improve it.
flow.say: Which idea kept the soil damp best? What would you change?
flow.kid: Did your design keep the soil damp? What would make it even better?
flow.think: A forest keeps its own air damp, because all the trees let out water together. Is a forest a bit like a giant plant sitter?
